title: Could some non-EU travellers soon avoid EES queues at Swiss airports?
desc:
Switzerland is considering a fast-track border scheme for selected non-EU travellers as authorities look for ways to reduce longer waiting times at airports following the introduction of Europe’s Entry/Exit System (EES).

The proposal was discussed this month, when Justice Minister Beat Jans met representatives of border control authorities, airlines and airports to consider ways of improving entry procedures.

The Swiss Federal Council said a so-called “National Facilitation Programme” (NFP) could offer a solution to the problem of lengthy EES border checks for non-EU nationals, which include Britons, Americans, Canadians and Australians.

Under the proposed arrangement, selected third-country nationals would voluntarily complete a one-time registration and screening process before travelling.

This could allow border officials to dispense with some routine questioning and carry out checks largely through automated e-gates, according to the Federal Council.

The authorities have not confirmed whether Switzerland will introduce the programme, or say who would qualify or when it could begin. The November meeting was intended to discuss possible improvements rather than announce a final decision.
summary: Switzerland is considering a fast-track border scheme for selected non-EU travellers as authorities look for ways to reduce longer waiting times at airports following the introduction of Europe’s Entry/Exit System (EES).

title: Why Austria's former foreign minister could lose her citizenship
desc:
Vienna's citizenship authority is looking into the case of Austria's former foreign minister Karin Kneissl, who now lives in Russia. The investigation concerns two provisions of Austria's strict citizenship laws.

Vienna's authorities are looking into whether former Austrian foreign minister Karin Kneissl should lose her Austrian citizenship following months of political controversy over her activities in Russia.

The municipal department responsible for immigration and citizenship (MA 35) is examining two possible legal grounds for the loss of her Austrian nationality, ORF reported .

Vienna's authorities are responsible for the case because Kneissl's last registered main residence in Austria was in the capital.

Kneissl was Austria's foreign minister from 2017 to 2019, having been nominated by the far-right Freedom Party of Austria (FPÖ), which was in a coalition with the centre-right Austrian People's Party (ÖVP).

She famously made international headlines in 2018 when she invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to her wedding in Styria and was photographed dancing with him.
summary: Vienna's citizenship authority is looking into the case of Austria's former foreign minister Karin Kneissl, who now lives in Russia. The investigation concerns two provisions of Austria's strict citizenship laws.

title: Everything to know about the Penedès: Spain's capital of cava
desc:
Cava is Spain’s answer to French Champagne – a sparkling wine that's typically golden in colour and enjoyed on special occasions. Here's what to know about it and how to visit the region it's made in.

Cava is made in various provinces around the country, including Tarragona, Girona, Lleida, Zaragoza, Badajoz, Navarra, Valencia, La Rioja and Álava, but the majority of it is produced in the Penedès, an undulating area of Catalonia, around one hour southwest of Barcelona.

There, it's made primarily from three native white grapes — Macabeo , Xarel·lo , and Parellada. These bubbles in the wine are the result of a second fermentation in the bottle, where carbon dioxide is generated.

Cava is left to age in the bottle for a minimum of nine months, while reserva varieties are left for 18 months and gran reserva for 30 months. It can be white or rosé and comes in varieties including Brut Nature , Extra Brut , and Brut, depending on the sugar content. Brut Nature has no added sugar, while Brut is sweeter.
summary: Cava is Spain’s answer to French Champagne – a sparkling wine that's typically golden in colour and enjoyed on special occasions. Here's what to know about it and how to visit the region it's made in.

title: Why the winter wardrobe switch in Norway is essential
desc:
Seasonal changes in Norway come quickly and can be intense, so your wardrobe and clothes need to keep up.

First, it helps you prepare physically and mentally for the darker months, and the colder weather that is coming to stay for a while.

Second, it is very practical, especially if you don’t have much storage space, as there’s no reason to let summer dresses or shorts take up room when you won’t use them for at least seven months.

It’s also a good way to remember what you own and what needs replacing, fixing, or finding a new home. For example, it’s easy to forget that your wool trousers tore last year and need fixing urgently before you cannot leave your home without them.

Space is one of the main reasons for the big wardrobe switch.

A light summer dress and a thin cardigan barely take up any room, but you will certainly need every inch of your closet for your wool base layers, your many jumpers and insulating mid-layers, and bulky outer layers. And that’s without counting the space you will need for all the extra accessories like hats, mittens, heavy scarves, and even your reflectors.
summary: Seasonal changes in Norway come quickly and can be intense, so your wardrobe and clothes need to keep up.

title: Life satisfaction in Germany declines for first time since 2021
desc:
For the first time since the Covid pandemic, fewer people in Germany say they are 'highly satisfied' with their lives compared to last year. Economic stagnation and dissatisfaction with income seems to be driving the trend.

Overall life satisfaction among people living in Germany declined this year compared to the year before, with economic concerns weighing heavily on morale, especially among women, young people and the unemployed.

This is the headline result of the SKL 'Happiness Atlas' ( Glücksatlas ) 2026, an annual report based on a series of 12 surveys which included a total of 12,461 people in Germany aged 16 or above.

Notably, self-reported life satisfaction scores for Germans and German residents fell overall.

Additionally the proportion of 'highly satisfied' individuals dropped from 48 to 44 percent, with a greater proportion of people instead stating that they felt 'moderately satisfied' with their lives.

Each year the SKL survey presents a sort-of happiness score for people in Germany – this is based on the average score of thousands of participants who are asked how satisfied they are with their life on a scale of zero (not at all satisfied) to 10 (completely satisfied).
summary: For the first time since the Covid pandemic, fewer people in Germany say they are 'highly satisfied' with their lives compared to last year. Economic stagnation and dissatisfaction with income seems to be driving the trend.

title: Is it really rude to say 'bon appétit' in France?
desc:
If you have ever shared a meal with French people, you have probably heard someone say bon appétit before starting to eat - so where does this idea come from that the phrase is rude?

The French expression, which literally translates as "good appetite" but really means 'enjoy your meal' or 'please enjoy' - has even been adopted into English, where it can sound rather fancy.

But did you know that, according to some, saying bon appétit is actually considered bad manners?

In traditional dining etiquette, it is seen as polite to wait until everyone has been served before starting to eat. In English, you might hear someone say "please, start" or "do start", while in a more informal setting, "dig in" is another common expression.

In France, however, the familiar bon appétit comes with a little controversy. The expression is perfectly correct French. The Académie française even includes it in its dictionary, defining it as an informal wish addressed to someone who is eating or about to eat.

The word appétit comes from the Latin appetitus , meaning "desire" or "strong craving", particularly when referring to food.
summary: If you have ever shared a meal with French people, you have probably heard someone say bon appétit before starting to eat - so where does this idea come from that the phrase is rude?

title: How much does a 'cheap date' really cost in Germany?
desc:
Dating in Munich, Berlin or Frankfurt costs more than €250 a go, according to research by Deutsche Bank. Here's which city costs most, why the prices are so high and how Germany compares with other European cities.

A new Europe-wide study has put a price on romance, and the news for Germany is not so bad actually.

The Cheap Date Index, part of Deutsche Bank Research Institute's Mapping the World's Prices 2026 report , compares 28 European cities. All three German cities on the list come in below the European average of €270.

And if you've got a steady job, take heart. Researchers cited by Euronews link financial security with relationship readiness, so a steady income may help your love life too.

If €250 sounds like quite an expensive date to you, note that we're not talking a bout a modest coffee date here. The index price is set based on the cost of; a bottle of wine, a mid-range dinner for two, two coffees, two cinema tickets, two single public transport tickets and a five kilometre taxi ride.
summary: Dating in Munich, Berlin or Frankfurt costs more than €250 a go, according to research by Deutsche Bank. Here's which city costs most, why the prices are so high and how Germany compares with other European cities.

title: Frenchman landed with €148k legal bill after train ticket fine
desc:
A man has told French media that he is being forced to sell his house after a €50 fine for travelling on a train without a valid ticket escalated into a €148,000 legal bill.

Arnaud, 39, who lives in the Bouches-du-Rhône département near Marseille has spoken out after losing the latest stage on his ongoing legal battle that all began when a ticket inspector attempted to fine him for travelling on a train without a valid ticket.

The bill, which was imposed by Mâcon Court in 2024 and upheld by Dijon Court of Appeal in 2025, has been brought to public attention this week after Arnaud told Le Parisien that he and his now-estranged wife are in the process of getting a divorce and selling their family home due to the ‘disproportionate’ sum he’s been told to pay.

The story began with the death of Arnaud’s grandmother in April 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic, when funerals had to take place within 24 hours due to the lockdown restrictions.

Arnaud boarded the TGV train from Aix-en-Provence to Paris, where the funeral was due to be held.
summary: A man has told French media that he is being forced to sell his house after a €50 fine for travelling on a train without a valid ticket escalated into a €148,000 legal bill.

title: Norway aims to put salmon farms on open seas
desc:
The Norwegian government proposed on Tuesday to start developing salmon farms on the open sea, away from the fjords and coastal pens where they are causing growing environmental and ecological damage.

Salmon farms are a major source of revenue and jobs for the Nordic country - fish products are its biggest export after oil and gas.

But packing the animals into cages almost always leads to sea lice outbreaks requiring treatments that can involve chemicals.

The lice can also infect wild salmon, whose numbers in Norwegian waterways have plunged in recent years.

The government wants to open three zones in the North and Norwegian Seas where farms could be placed in deeper waters to limit lice as well as excessive excrement and nutrients in the water.

That can foster plant and algae growth that removes oxygen and threatens other fish.

"Pisciculture on the sea could be a significant contributor to value creation along our coasts in the coming years," Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said in a statement.
summary: The Norwegian government proposed on Tuesday to start developing salmon farms on the open sea, away from the fjords and coastal pens where they are causing growing environmental and ecological damage.

title: Swedish Moderate leader given an extra week so Centre can test Social Democrats' offer
desc:
Sweden's parliamentary speaker Andreas Norlén has given Ulf Kristersson, leader of the Moderate Party, an additional week to see whether the government solution the Social Democrats promised the Centre Party is viable before his candidacy as prime minister be put to the parliament for a vote.

Kristersson met the parliament's speaker, Andreas Norlén, on Tuesday afternoon to discuss the progress of his sonderingsuppdrag , the task of forming Sweden's next government.

After the meeting Kristersson said that his interpretation of the Centre Party's decision to choose the Social Democrats' 'total package' over the rival offer made by the Moderate Party, was that it was only provisional and depended on the Social Democrats successfully convincing the Left Party to accept a government in which it has no ministers.

“On Sunday, the Centre Party announced that it was unable to choose between the two proposals because it still didn’t know whether all the parties on the left supported the proposal submitted by the Social Democrats, whether the Left Party was sticking to its demand to be part of the government, or whether the Left Party and the Green Party supported the policies contained in that proposal," he said.
summary: Sweden's parliamentary speaker Andreas Norlén has given Ulf Kristersson, leader of the Moderate Party, an additional week to see whether the government solution the Social Democrats promised the Centre Party is viable before his candidacy as prime minister be put to the parliament for a vote.

title: Danish word of the day: sprogøre
desc:
Photo by Francesco Ungaro on Unsplash and Nicolas Raymond/FlickR

If you’ve developed a good grasp of Danish or other languages, don’t be surprised if someone compliments you on your ‘language ear’.

A sprogøre refers to a “language ear” and is a compound of the two words. It’s used to compliment someone’s ability to learn, understand and speak languages.

Someone with a good ‘language ear’ will not only pick up the basics but also nail the trickier aspects, such as accent and intonation.

Therefore, if you have a Danish sprogøre , you will probably be able to tell regional dialects apart. Things like grammar probably also come a lot easier.

A person with a good ear for languages is also adept at getting a grip on new languages.

When it comes to having a good language ear yourself, it can be a good mix of natural gifts and hard work.

If you’ve already put in the work and learned one additional language, then picking up others should be easier. This is especially true if the new language you are learning has a lot in common with the one you already speak.
summary: If you’ve developed a good grasp of Danish or other languages, don’t be surprised if someone compliments you on your ‘language ear’.

title: What we know about five EU countries' planned Rwanda migrant deportation centre
desc:
On Monday, Denmark, Austria, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced a plan to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, the first such facility outside the EU. Here is what we know about the "return-hub" initiative.

The five have been exploring sending migrants to centres outside Europe for months, with the pilot project planned to be launched next year.

During a joint press announcement in Vienna, ministers from the five EU countries and Rwanda remained evasive on the project's scope.

But according to people involved, the centre will be for around 100 migrants.

They will be men and women whose asylum applications have been rejected but who refuse to return to their countries of origin despite having exhausted all avenues of appeal.

Nationals of any country are eligible, without exceptions, according to those involved in the plan. Minors are excluded.

NGOs are worried the initiative could ultimately target all asylum seekers -- a claim denied by the five countries involved.

The five European countries' national authorities will be responsible for transferring the rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.
summary: On Monday, Denmark, Austria, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced a plan to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, the first such facility outside the EU. Here is what we know about the "return-hub" initiative.

title: Black Friday: Know your consumer rights when shopping in Denmark
desc:
Black Friday emails have already started hitting our inboxes, so it's a good idea to know your rights in Denmark for when things go wrong if you are planning on trying to bag a good deal.

In Denmark you have several protections as a shopper, some covered by EU law, some under Danish consumer law, and some at the discretion of the individual retailer.

Here are some of the most important, which come in particularly handy around Black Friday, if you accidentally pick something up you don't want to keep.

If a retailer offers åbent køb , this means you can return an item after buying it, even if there is no defect.

There is no legal requirement to offer this as an option, but many Danish retailers, such as clothes retailers like Nelly or Vero Moda, or the electric goods retailer Elgiganten, do offer it.

They will usually display information about åbent køb on signs in the shop itself and on the purchase receipt, and if you're not sure, you can ask if it's offered (ideally, ask before you pay).

It may also only apply for some items – underwear and jewellery are often not included for hygiene reasons, for example.
summary: Black Friday emails have already started hitting our inboxes, so it's a good idea to know your rights in Denmark for when things go wrong if you are planning on trying to bag a good deal.

title: Italy takes record €1.2bn in tourist tax as councils face questions over spending
desc:
Figures reported on Monday showed councils on course to collect record revenues from local taxes levied on visitors in 2026, though where all that money goes is often far from clear.

The record total was almost 17 times what councils collected from the imposta di soggiorno ( tourist tax on overnight stays) in 2011, when it was first introduced by just 13 councils.

By 2026 the number had risen to 1,411, according to tourism consultancy JFC. Rome remained by far the biggest earner, taking around a quarter of all revenue in the first half of this year, it said.

By law, councils are supposed to spend the revenue money directly on tourism, cultural heritage, the environment and local public services.

But in practice it often goes straight into their general budgets, in breach of the law, consumer group Codacons warned on Tuesday in response to the latest figures .

“There’s a complete lack of transparency over where the money raised through the tourist tax actually goes, and nobody knows how councils use the funds, with a real risk that the revenue is being used to cover holes in their budgets,” the group stated.
summary: Figures reported on Monday showed councils on course to collect record revenues from local taxes levied on visitors in 2026, though where all that money goes is often far from clear.

title: Price of public transport in eastern Denmark set to rise in 2027
desc:
On January 17th, the average price of a public transport ticket will rise in eastern Denmark, according to Danish public transport group Din Offentlige Transport (DOT), which covers Zealand, Falster, Lolland and Møn.

Prices are set to rise by 0.7 percent on average across all transport types due to a yearly adjustment designed to cover the rising cost of running public transport, DOT said in a press release.

Most travellers will not notice a difference, or if there is a price difference, it will be minimal, DOT said.

The rise will be most noticeable for commuters and pensioners, with the price of the 2-7 zone commuter card rising by between 5 and 10 kroner, and the price of the three-month pensioner card rising by between 20 and 60 kroner depending on the type of card.

"Despite rising running costs and energy costs over the past few years, we're keeping increases to prices on public transport at a low level," Jens Visholm, chair of the DOT group and commercial director of rail agency DSB said in the press release.
summary: On January 17th, the average price of a public transport ticket will rise in eastern Denmark, according to Danish public transport group Din Offentlige Transport (DOT), which covers Zealand, Falster, Lolland and Møn.

title: Will Spain's golden visa scheme be brought back by a right-wing government?
desc:
Almost two years since the elimination of the golden visa, The Local spoke to a legal expert on her opinion as to whether any new right-wing government would bring it back again.

It has now been one year and seven months since Spain's golden visa programme was abolished. The visa allowed non-EU citizens to gain residency in Spain by either buying property worth €500,000, investing €1 million in shares in Spanish companies, €2 million in government bonds, or transferring €1 million to a Spanish bank account.

The visa was axed in order to help solve the housing crisis as foreign investors were being blamed for pushing up housing prices and squeezing locals out of the market.

Has abolishing the visa actually helped the situation though and is there a chance that it could be brought back again?

If the polls are to be believed, the centre-right Partido Popular (PP) will win the next general election in Spain on November 29th, but fall short of an overall majority, meaning that it will likely seek a coalition with far-right party Vox.
summary: Almost two years since the elimination of the golden visa, The Local spoke to a legal expert on her opinion as to whether any new right-wing government would bring it back again.

title: 'An extra election in Sweden is now a plausible scenario'
desc:
In today's Sweden in Focus Extra podcast, political scientist Nicholas Aylott gives us his analysis of Sweden's post-election drama.

Not yet a member of The Local? Join now with this special offer for podcast listeners .

Moderate Party leader and current acting Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has been tasked by the Speaker with forming a government.

However, Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson seems to have the edge over him after the Centre Party announced that it was choosing to continue negotiations with her rather than with the parties of the right.

But all is far from sewn up. The big sticking point remains the Centre Party's refusal to accept a government in which the Left Party has ministers. Nooshi Dadgostar's Left Party in turn has given no indication that it is ready to give up its demands.

Nicholas Aylott , associate politics professor at Södertörn University, gives his views in a conversation with The Local's James Savage .

Join the conversation in our comments section below. Share your own views and experience and if you have a question or suggestion for our journalists then email us at news@thelocal.se . Please keep comments civil, constructive and on topic – and make sure to read our terms of use before getting involved.
summary: In today's Sweden in Focus Extra podcast, political scientist Nicholas Aylott gives us his analysis of Sweden's post-election drama.

title: Swedish parties agree details of new law to stop deportations
desc:
All parties in the Swedish parliament apart from the far-right Sweden Democrats have agreed on the scope of a new law to stop the deportations of young adults who came to Sweden as dependents.

The Social Insurance Committee, which handles migration law, on Tuesday adopted a decision setting out the scope of the new law, which will apply to all people who came to Sweden as dependents of their parents whose residence permits were then rejected on or after July 20th 2021, and whose parents remain in Sweden.

The Social Democrats, Centre Party, Green Party, Left Party, Moderate Party, Liberal Party and Christian Democrats all agreed on the provisions of the new law. The aim to draft the full text of the law in the coming months within the committee, as there is currently no government in place.

"There is a majority in the parliament to put a stop to the deportations of teenagers," Annika Hirvonen, immigration spokesperson for the Green Party, said in a statement.

Today, the Social Insurance Committee reached an agreement on a clear scope and a policy decision - a crucial step toward implementing this legislation. The law concerns the lives of nearly a thousand people, as well as their opportunity to live a secure life.
summary: All parties in the Swedish parliament apart from the far-right Sweden Democrats have agreed on the scope of a new law to stop the deportations of young adults who came to Sweden as dependents.

title: Danish economy to outperform rest of EU this year, new forecast reveals
desc:
A new economic forecast from the EU Commission sees Denmark performing the best out of all 27 member countries, predicting growth of 4.5 percent for the year 2026.

Denmark is the only country in the EU Commission's forecast to see predicted GDP growth above 4 percent this year, followed by Slovenia and Malta (both 3.9 percent), Poland (3.5 percent) and Cyprus (3.4 percent).

The EU 27 average is just 1.4 percent, while the Eurozone average is 1.2 percent growth for the year 2026.

"The Danish economy is doing significantly better than our European neighbours," Allan Sørensen, head economist at the Confederation of Danish Industry, told public broadcaster DR.

"Luckily we have a strong medical industry which is securing high growth in the Danish economy. If we exclude the medical industry, however, growth is not as high."

Denmark's predicted growth in 2026 is, however, much higher than the country's forecast for 2027 and 2028 (2 percent and 2.1 percent respectively).

According to the report, the 2026 rate is due in the most part to net exports, and it predicts that the country's economy will slow down in 2027 and 2028, with exports taken over by domestic demand.
summary: A new economic forecast from the EU Commission sees Denmark performing the best out of all 27 member countries, predicting growth of 4.5 percent for the year 2026.

title: Swiss airline to launch new daily flight between Zurich and London
desc:
A Swiss airline is adding a new UK destination to its network with flights to begin in spring 2027.

Chair Airlines will launch the new route on May 27th, connecting Switzerland’s largest city Zurich with Southend Airport in Essex.

Southend airport stands around 35 miles (56 km) east of central London. Tickets for the flights went on sale on November 16th, 2026.

Unlike London’s larger airports, Southend offers a smaller and potentially less hectic arrival point for travellers, and it has a railway station directly opposite its terminal, with direct trains taking around 52 minutes to reach London's Liverpool Street rail station.

The new connection will give travellers from Switzerland another option for visiting the British capital, as well as providing easier access to Essex and the wider south-east of England; and vice versa, it will make it more convenient for British visitors to travel to Zurich and explore Switzerland’s mountain and ski destinations.

Chair Airlines chief executive Shpend Ibrahimi said the airline had considered several airport options before settling on Southend, pointing to its shorter distances, efficient airport operations and direct rail connection to the capital.
summary: A Swiss airline is adding a new UK destination to its network with flights to begin in spring 2027.

title: Language tips: How to understand fast-spoken French
desc:
It's the despairing cry of many French learners - why won't the French just slow down to give you a chance of understanding them? We asked French language coach Llyane Stanfield for some tips.

This is one of the most common frustrations I hear from people learning French, especially those who have moved to France.

You may recognise hundreds of French words on paper, yet struggle to understand those same words when a neighbour starts chatting or a waiter asks an unexpected question.

And what’s the first thing you turn to? Things that help you listen better - you watch TV, play podcasts, surround yourself with the language.

And those things can easily become background noise. They may familiarise you with French, but they don't train your brain to produce the words and sentences you need in conversations.

That's why you need to start SPEAKING French, so your brain learns to recognise those same words and sentences when others say them.

When you say a French word or phrase out loud, you are doing more than practising pronunciation.
summary: It's the despairing cry of many French learners - why won't the French just slow down to give you a chance of understanding them? We asked French language coach Llyane Stanfield for some tips.

title: Switzerland set to make switching health insurance easier
desc:
Switzerland could soon make it easier to switch basic health insurers, under a proposal that would allow customers to cancel and change providers entirely online.

Switzerland's Federal Council has recommended that parliament accept a motion by Green Liberal National Council member Patrick Hässig that would change the way people can switch health insurance providers.

This motion would require all health insurers to offer the same standardised, fully digital process for cancelling an existing policy and signing up with a new provider.

The aim is to reduce administrative hurdles and make it easier for policyholders to shop around.

The proposal comes as health insurance premiums continue to rise, with premiums set to increase by an average of 5 percent in 2027 , bringing the average monthly premium to 412 Swiss francs, according to the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH). And yet, only 7.5 percent of insured people switched providers at the beginning of 2025, according to the FOPH’s latest figures.
summary: Switzerland could soon make it easier to switch basic health insurers, under a proposal that would allow customers to cancel and change providers entirely online.

title: How could Norway's plan to raise retirement age affect you?
desc:
On Tuesday morning, the Norwegian government announced plans to gradually increase the country’s retirement age so that it rises alongside life expectancy. How much longer will you have to work before drawing a pension in Norway in the future?

Minister of Employment and Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng said in a press release that the government is proposing changes to the retirement age so that people remain active in the workforce for longer in order to help secure the welfare state and protect future pension payments.

"We live longer, and most of us stay healthy for more years. Therefore, we also have to work a little longer if the pension system is to last for our children and grandchildren. At the same time, we propose a better social structure and better regulation of minimum benefits in the future. In sum, this makes the pension system fairer," Stenseng said.

Currently, most people in Norway can start taking a pension at 62 (provided they have built up enough pension entitlements) and everyone gets one by 67.
summary: On Tuesday morning, the Norwegian government announced plans to gradually increase the country’s retirement age so that it rises alongside life expectancy. How much longer will you have to work before drawing a pension in Norway in the future?

title: Why some French residents are receiving letters about having a baby
desc:
Young women and men across France are being sent letters from the government throughout November, informing them about the steps they can take to preserve their fertility.

Letters are to be sent to all 29-year-old men and women in France by the end of November 2026, to raise awareness of fertility issues and provide guidance on preserving fertility.

It's the first public campaign to be launched since the government announced its fertility plan ( plan fertilité ) in February and coincides with Infertility Awareness Month ( Mois de sensibilisation à l'infertilité ).

The letter reminds recipients that fertility declines from age 30 in women and age 40 in men. It also highlights the potential impact of medical issues, diet and unhealthy habits such as smoking on a couple's ability to conceive.

In France, 15 to 25 percent of couples - more than 3 million people - wishing to conceive a child encounter difficulties.

Health minister, Stéphanie Rist, said in a statement that the aim of the letters, which are being sent via the country’s health insurance platform, Assurance Maladie, is to "give every adult the means to understand and preserve their fertility".
summary: Young women and men across France are being sent letters from the government throughout November, informing them about the steps they can take to preserve their fertility.

title: Germany and Norway to buy more US air defences for Ukraine
desc:
Germany and Norway will fund a new package of US Patriot air defences for Ukraine, Germany's defence minister said Tuesday, as Kyiv struggles to defend against Russia's onslaught.

"Russia is intensifying its air attacks because it is not making progress on the battlefield," minister Boris Pistorius said at an EU meeting in Brussels.

Pistorius said that Berlin would contribute $300 million to buying the latest tranche of US weaponry – with the focus of the package on air defence, and in particular Patriot interceptor missiles.

Russia has stepped up its bombing campaign on cities and infrastructure around Ukraine in what Kyiv says is an attempt to freeze the country into submission this winter.

Ukraine has desperately been urging its backers to help find more Patriots as they are the only system capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles.

Kyiv has been facing a dire shortfall as US stockpiles have been drained by the war with Iran.

The announcement of fresh support comes ahead of a meeting of Ukraine's military backers at NATO headquarters in Brussels later on Tuesday.
summary: Germany and Norway will fund a new package of US Patriot air defences for Ukraine, Germany's defence minister said Tuesday, as Kyiv struggles to defend against Russia's onslaught.

title: Five practical things foreigners should consider before moving to Austria for work
desc:
Many people from outside the EU dream of living and working in Austria – but they may wonder what practical steps they should take. The Local spoke to the Austrian Business Agency to find out the biggest factors to consider and how to overcome hurdles.

For international residents who want a high quality of life combined with stunning nature, Austria is up there as a dream destination. But just how hard is it to find work and make the move to the country successfully?

The Local spoke with Margit Kreuzhuber, head of Work in Austria at the Austrian Business Agency (ABA), which helps companies attract international skilled workers and offers free support to professionals making the move to Austria.

Here's a look at five key things non-EU nationals should consider if they want to settle in the Alpine nation.

Austria is suffering from a skilled worker shortage that will only get worse as more people retire.

That means there are plenty of opportunities out there for qualified non-EU professionals.
summary: Many people from outside the EU dream of living and working in Austria – but they may wonder what practical steps they should take. The Local spoke to the Austrian Business Agency to find out the biggest factors to consider and how to overcome hurdles.

title: Flights, trains, schools: How Italy will be hit by strikes and protests this weekend
desc:
Transport, schools and healthcare could all be disrupted by staff walkouts and demonstrations across Italy starting on Friday, November 20th and extending into the weekend.

Italy's 'autumn of discontent' continues this weekend with rallies protesting high living costs and demanding better funding of public services as parliament debates the 2027 budget bill.

Student protests are set to take place alongside a national general strike on Friday, November 20th, while transport services are likely to be affected from Friday into Saturday and Sunday.

Friday’s strike was planned by Italy’s largest trade union, Cgil, to coincide with protests by students as part of a Europe-wide International Youth Strike day.

The day-long walkout is set to affect all sectors apart from air and rail transport, after Italy’s strike regulator ruled against their inclusion, according to La Repubblica.

Some local public transport operators, including Milan’s ATM, Venice’s Atvo, and EAV and ANM in Naples, have also reportedly been excluded from Friday’s general strike.
summary: Transport, schools and healthcare could all be disrupted by staff walkouts and demonstrations across Italy starting on Friday, November 20th and extending into the weekend.

title: Swedish electricity prices could edge above 2022 energy crisis levels this winter
desc:
Swedish electricity is expected to get unusually expensive this winter – even more so than during the 2022-2023 energy crisis, according to a new forecast.

Households and businesses in southern Sweden – where German and Danish electricity prices spill over into the Swedish market – are expected to be hit the hardest.

Nordic electricity prices are forecast to average around 1.70 kronor per kilowatt-hour between December and February, according to electricity retailer Bixia.

That would be "slightly higher" than the levels seen during the 2022-2023 winter season, the company wrote in a press release.

THE LOCAL'S GUIDE: How to save money on your energy bill in Sweden

In electricity price zone SE4 – which covers Skåne, Blekinge and parts of Halland and Småland – prices are expected to reach 1.80 kronor per kilowatt-hour over the winter months.

In SE3 – which includes Stockholm and Gothenburg as well as the Mälardalen region – the forecast points to 1.50 kronor.

Meanwhile, zones SE1 and SE2 – essentially everything north of the Dalälven river – are expected to see significantly lower prices at around 0.70 kronor.
summary: Swedish electricity is expected to get unusually expensive this winter – even more so than during the 2022-2023 energy crisis, according to a new forecast.

title: French Expression of the Day: Être à la masse
desc:
This French expression may have origins linked to electrical wiring.

This French expression is good to know if you're ever feeling disconnected.

The expression être à la masse , roughly pronounced eh-truh ah lah mass (listen here ), describes someone who is confused, exhausted or overwhelmed by what's happening around them. Depending on the context, it can also mean being a bit dazed or acting irrationally.

The exact origin of the expression is uncertain, but two main theories are commonly put forward.

One explanation links the expression to electricity. In electrical engineering, an appliance that is à la masse is connected to the earth through a conductor. Figuratively, the expression may evoke the image of an electrical short circuit or a faulty appliance that is no longer working properly. Applied to a person, it suggests someone who is disconnected from the world around them or whose thinking is not functioning as it should.

Another theory relates it to the tool known as a masse (sledgehammer). The idea is that taking a blow to the head with a heavy hammer would leave someone dazed, confused or unable to think clearly.
summary: This French expression may have origins linked to electrical wiring.

title: Seven in 10 immigrants in Germany in work but pay gaps remain
desc:
More immigrants are working than ever, but they still earn less on average than workers without an immigrant background, and many worry more about their jobs.

Seven in 10 immigrants in Germany aged 15 to 64 now have a job, new statistics show. This represents a 13-point jump from 57 percent in 2005.

The figures come from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) and feature in Germany’s latest integration report , a biennial report by the German Centre for Integration and Migration Research.

The same figures show that people without an immigrant background have moved up too, from 68 to 81 percent over the same time period.

Of the 52.7 million people in Germany aged 15 to 64, 12.8 million (24 percent) are immigrants. Another 3.2 million are the children of two immigrant parents, and 2.5 million have one immigrant parent.

The steepest climb is among the children of immigrants. The employment rate among people with two immigrant parents went from 47 to 70 percent. Among people with one immigrant parent it went from 48 to 72 percent.
summary: More immigrants are working than ever, but they still earn less on average than workers without an immigrant background, and many worry more about their jobs.

title: Airbus to create 700 jobs with new factory in south-west France
desc:
European aircraft manufacturer Airbus has announced plans to build a new factory near Toulouse, south-west France, creating 700 jobs by 2031 as it expands production capacity.

The new industrial site will cover 48 hectares between Cornebarrieu and Colomiers, northwest of Toulouse. It will be dedicated to manufacturing engine pylons - the structures that connect an aircraft's engines to its wings.

The factory will complement Airbus's existing Saint-Eloi facility in Toulouse, which is currently operating at full capacity amid an order backlog of 9,300 aircraft.

The new site will employ around 3,500 people in total, including 700 newly created positions. The investment is expected to amount to between €600 million and €900 million.

The announcement has been welcomed by trade unions, particularly because production will remain in the Toulouse area.

"It's excellent news," Florent Veletchy, a central representative for the CFTC union, told local broadcaster ICI Occitanie.

"We are investing between €600 million and €900 million in a site here, creating jobs here. That's a good thing. Above all, what matters to us is that the site is in Toulouse. We would have viewed it very negatively if it had been moved to another city or another country."
summary: European aircraft manufacturer Airbus has announced plans to build a new factory near Toulouse, south-west France, creating 700 jobs by 2031 as it expands production capacity.

title: Train strike leaves thousands stranded in Spain as minimum services fail
desc:
Commuter rail services in Madrid and Barcelona have been "severely disrupted" this Tuesday as minimum services haven't been met.

Spain is facing another day of rail stoppages this Tuesday November 17th, after unions called a 24-hour strike.

Although minimum services had been established, Renfe reported early Tuesday morning that they are not being met on the Madrid commuter rail network and is recommending that passengers seek alternative methods of transport.

The same is happening in Catalonia, where only half of the scheduled Rodalies commuter trains are running.

The director of Rodalies, Òscar Playà, reported that 40 percent of the trains scheduled for the minimum service during Tuesday's rail strike are not running.

The Catalan government considers the latest breach of minimum service requirements on the commuter rail network "unacceptable”.

The Minister of Territory and government spokesperson, Silvia Paneque, told 'El Matí de Catalunya Ràdio' that the government "will take action" to ensure that Renfe opens the necessary investigations.
summary: Commuter rail services in Madrid and Barcelona have been "severely disrupted" this Tuesday as minimum services haven't been met.

title: Today in Norway: A roundup of the latest news on Tuesday
desc:
The Norwegian government plans to raise the retirement age, Norway faces greatest risk of a nuclear accident in 40 years, household finances are worse now than a few years ago, and more news on Tuesday.

Major shake-up of Norway’s pension system: Government plans to raise the retirement age

On Tuesday morning, the Norwegian government a nnounced plans to gradually increase the country’s retirement age so that it rises alongside life expectancy.

"We live longer, and most of us stay healthy for more years. Therefore, we also have to work a little longer if the pension system is to last for our children and grandchildren. At the same time, we propose a better social structure and better regulation of minimum benefits in the future. In sum, this makes the pension system fairer," said Minister of Employment and Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng in a press release.

Currently, most people in Norway can start taking a pension at 62, and everyone gets one by 67. The new plan would replace the fixed age of 67 with a flexible "standard retirement age" that goes up by about one year every decade.
summary: The Norwegian government plans to raise the retirement age, Norway faces greatest risk of a nuclear accident in 40 years, household finances are worse now than a few years ago, and more news on Tuesday.

title: Greenland's 'fatherless' sue the Danish state
desc:
A trial opens on Tuesday in Denmark where a group of Greenlanders are suing the state, saying their rights were violated when they could not legally establish their filiation to their Danish fathers.

Between 1938 and 1963 in western Greenland, and until 1974 in the rest of the territory, children born out of wedlock to a Danish father did not have their paternity legally recognised, unlike children living in Denmark.

The 26 plaintiffs argue this difference in treatment, based on their origin, constituted discrimination and deprived them among other things of their inheritance.

According to an estimate by the Danish Ministry of Social Affairs, 8,000 people born between 1911 and 1974 in Greenland can be considered "legally fatherless".

Mads Pramming, the lawyer representing the 26 plaintiffs, is optimistic.

"The case is very strong when it comes to human rights," he told AFP.

Klaus Frederiksen is one of the spokespeople for the "legally fatherless". He has come to Copenhagen for the trial and is due to testify on Wednesday.
summary: A trial opens on Tuesday in Denmark where a group of Greenlanders are suing the state, saying their rights were violated when they could not legally establish their filiation to their Danish fathers.

title: Mobile phones in Sweden will suddenly beep loudly on December 7th
desc:
If you suddenly get a loud emergency alert to your phone on December 7th – don't worry, it's just a test.

Sweden is set to test its new mobile emergency alert system, called SE-Alert, on December 7th.

The test will take place at 3pm alongside the quarterly test of the outdoor emergency siren " Hesa Fredrik ".

This means that if you have an up-to-date smartphone which is switched on and connected to a mobile network, you should receive a pop-up text notification accompanied by a loud audio signal and vibration, even if you've got your phone on silent.

If you don't want to receive the alert, you should completely switch off your phone.

It's just a test and you don't need to do anything – but it will be sent out to everyone, including children, the elderly and international tourists who just happen to be in Sweden, so it's worth informing friends and family members of the test in advance if you think they may otherwise get concerned or caught off guard by receiving the notification.

It will be sent out to everyone in Sweden regardless of whether you have a Swedish or international number, the Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency – which is responsible for the test – has previously confirmed to The Local.
summary: If you suddenly get a loud emergency alert to your phone on December 7th – don't worry, it's just a test.

title: Tesla makes major investment to expand German factory
desc:
US electric carmaker Tesla said Monday it will invest three billion euros to expand its German factory, which it claims will have capacity to produce one million driverless Cybercabs annually.

The investment at the only European factory run by Elon Musk's company stands in stark contrast to other players in Germany's struggling auto sector, which have been downsizing aggressively.

The expansion also comes despite resistance from residents and activists worried about the environmental impact, and with billionaire Musk increasingly controversial in Germany due to his backing of the far right in last year's elections.

"This will lay the foundation for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Gruenheide," a town outside Berlin, the company said in a statement announcing the investment.

Tesla's Gruenheide "Gigafactory" was opened in 2022 after a tumultuous two-year approval and construction process, and was given permission to expand by local authorities two years ago.

But the manufacturer scaled back some of its original plans after local residents opposed them in a non-binding poll, with concerns including proposals to raze large areas of woodland and increased traffic in the area.
summary: US electric carmaker Tesla said Monday it will invest three billion euros to expand its German factory, which it claims will have capacity to produce one million driverless Cybercabs annually.

title: Today in Austria: A roundup of the latest news on Tuesday
desc:
A foreign student has been banned from working after helping out at another restaurant branch in Vienna and a former minister could lose her Austrian citizenship, plus more stories from Austria on Tuesday.

Foreign student loses right to work after helping out at another restaurant branch

The Austrian National Union of Students (ÖH) has lodged a complaint about a Filipino student at the University of Vienna whose right to work was withdrawn after a period of work at another branch of a restaurant.

According to the student union, the woman had a work permit for her job in the restaurant. When her employer opened a second branch, she was asked to work there for a month.

According to the ÖH, Austria's Public Employment Service (AMS) found a breach of employment law because the second branch was registered as a separate company. The student union argues that the woman wasn't informed of the change and shouldn't be held responsible.

Vienna's opposition parties took aim at the city's immigration and citizenship authority (MA 35) during a special sitting of the provincial parliament on Monday. The discussion focused on delays in processing applications and allegations of corruption.
summary: A foreign student has been banned from working after helping out at another restaurant branch in Vienna and a former minister could lose her Austrian citizenship, plus more stories from Austria on Tuesday.

title: Today in Switzerland: A roundup of the latest news on Tuesday
desc:
Switching health insurance plans could become much simpler; online shopping fraud poses the most common cyber risk in Switzerland; plus other news in our Tuesday roundup.

Despite continued hikes in health insurance premiums, few policyholders actually switch providers to save money: only 8 percent do so each year.

The main reason cited for this reluctance to change carriers is the complexity of the administrative procedures involved in the switch.

This process will, however, become simpler: the Federal Council has proposed accepting a parliamentary motion aimed at establishing a fully digital and standardised insurance termination process, designed to make the transition from one insurance company to another easier that it is currently.

Online shopping fraud poses the most common cyber risk in Switzerland, new study reveals

According to a new study released on Monday by Bâloise Helvetia insurance company, online shopping fraud “is the most common type of cybercrime” in the country.

“Many cybercrimes today do not start with a technical attack, but with a seemingly attractive sales offer,” the study found.
summary: Switching health insurance plans could become much simpler; online shopping fraud poses the most common cyber risk in Switzerland; plus other news in our Tuesday roundup.

title: Today in Spain: A roundup of the latest news on Tuesday
desc:
Rosalía makes history at the Grammys with 9 nominations, police search for fugitive from Oviedo bombing in Barcelona, 22-year-old woman arrested in Madrid for stabbing boyfriend and more news from Spain this Tuesday November 17th.

The Spanish singer Rosalía has made history at the Grammys by becoming the second most nominated artist of this edition with 9 nominations, well above other stars such as Taylor Swift , Madonna and Olivia Rodrigo , and only falling behind Raye, who has 11 nominations.

This means the artist is now the Spanish artist with the most nominations in a single year , and the third in total behind Plácido Domingo, who had 31 nominations, and Alicia de Larrocha who had 14, and above Alejandro Sanz and Julio Iglesias who each had 7.

Until now, only two Spanish-language albums had been nominated for Album of the Year, both by Bad Bunny.

A police operation with the Guardia Civil and Mossos d'Esquadra was launched in the province of Barcelona on Monday morning following a call from someone reporting that they had seen an individual in Manresa who could be "El Ruso ", the fugitive from Oviedo accused of planting a bomb that killed one national police officer and seriously injured another last week in the Asturian capital.
summary: Rosalía makes history at the Grammys with 9 nominations, police search for fugitive from Oviedo bombing in Barcelona, 22-year-old woman arrested in Madrid for stabbing boyfriend and more news from Spain this Tuesday November 17th.

title: Sweden's Princess Estelle has work experience placement with Finnish president
desc:
Sweden's Princess Estelle – just like the rest of Sweden's other year eight pupils – is out on a two-week work placement this autumn, but instead of sweeping floors at her local ICA supermarket, she's now shadowing Finnish President Alexander Stubb.

Estelle (14) started her work experience – known in Sweden as prao ( praktisk arbetslivsorientering , practical working life orientation) – last week.

In the first week, she interned with her grandfather, King Carl XVI Gustaf, at the Royal Palace, where she shadowed his schedule and visited various departments within the Royal Court, the palace stated in a press release.

This week, the court added, she is at the Swedish embassy in Helsinki, where she will learn more about the Swedish foreign service and the work of a diplomatic mission abroad.

In addition, she will spend a couple of days at the office of the President in Helsinki to shadow the Finnish head of state, Alexander Stubb, in his official duties.

During her prao at the Royal Palace in Stockholm, Princess Estelle met the British artist Andy Goldsworthy, who was installing a sculpture in Kungliga Djurgården, the royal park in central Stockholm.
summary: Sweden's Princess Estelle – just like the rest of Sweden's other year eight pupils – is out on a two-week work placement this autumn, but instead of sweeping floors at her local ICA supermarket, she's now shadowing Finnish President Alexander Stubb.

title: French cricket 'dying' as federation crisis and chaos deepens
desc:
Cricket in France is at risk of disappearing altogether, less than two years before the sport makes its long-awaited Olympic return.

The last, and only time that cricket was played at the Olympics was in Paris in 1900, where England beat France by 158 runs to win the gold medal.

France will not be at the Twenty20 tournament at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and cricket in the country is on the verge of "dying" due to a crisis within the country's federation, Miriam Romero, a player and administrator, told AFP.

Clubs suspended the national league this year as they try to force president Prebagarane 'Prebou' Balane to resign following a series of scandals.

The organisation lost its recognition by France's sports ministry early this year, while the International Cricket Council (ICC) in June suspended development funding and placed France Cricket on notice for "non-compliance with membership criteria".

This came after scandals such as 'ghost' women's matches and development funding that was unaccounted for.
summary: Cricket in France is at risk of disappearing altogether, less than two years before the sport makes its long-awaited Olympic return.

title: Today in Germany: A roundup of the latest news on Tuesday
desc:
Tesla to invest three billion euros in German 'Gigafactory', right-wing extremists 'well-established' in Thuringia, Wirtz scores twice as Germany thrash Netherlands 5-0 and more news on Tuesday, November 17th.

Tuesday's top story: Tesla to invest three billion euros in German 'Gigafactory'

Tesla will invest three billion euros to expand its Grünheide "Gigafactory" outside Berlin, the company said on Monday. A new facility will eventually produce up to one million driverless Cybercabs a year, with construction due to begin in the first half of 2027 and production in 2029.

The move contrasts sharply with the rest of Germany's struggling auto sector. Volkswagen is cutting tens of thousands of jobs, and Mercedes said last week it would halt all investment in Germany and was weighing factory closures.

The Grünheide plant opened in 2022 after a tumultuous approval process. Tesla scaled back some plans after residents opposed them in a non-binding poll, and activists camped in treehouses to block expansion.
summary: Tesla to invest three billion euros in German 'Gigafactory', right-wing extremists 'well-established' in Thuringia, Wirtz scores twice as Germany thrash Netherlands 5-0 and more news on Tuesday, November 17th.

title: Apple faces Paris trial over alleged planned obsolescence of iPhones
desc:
Apple will stand trial in Paris in June 2027 on suspicion of having organised the planned obsolescence of several iPhone models by preventing repairs outside official outlets, a source close to the case told AFP on Tuesday.

The case brought by French prosecutors against the US tech giant on charges of "obstructing repair and refurbishment" is a first, the campaign group Stop Planned Obsolescence said, welcoming the move after filing a complaint in December 2022.

"We strongly contest these unfounded allegations," Apple said when contacted by AFP.

Planned obsolescence refers to techniques used by manufacturers to deliberately shorten the lifespan of their products, generally electronic devices, thereby encouraging consumers to replace them more frequently.

If found guilty, Apple could be fined up to €300,000 or a percentage of its annual revenue, and could face compensation claims from clients.

According to the source close to the case, Apple Distribution International and its parent company Apple Inc are to appear in court for a four-day trial starting on June 17th.
summary: Apple will stand trial in Paris in June 2027 on suspicion of having organised the planned obsolescence of several iPhone models by preventing repairs outside official outlets, a source close to the case told AFP on Tuesday.

title: Today in Denmark: A roundup of the latest news on Tuesday
desc:
Half of Denmark's drivers set to pay more for owning their vehicles next year, Black Friday shoppers warned to look out for scams and more news from Denmark on Tuesday.

Price of public transport in eastern Denmark set to rise next year

On January 17th, the average price of a public transport ticket will rise in eastern Denmark, according to Danish public transport company Din Offentlige Transport (DOT), which covers Zealand, Falster, Lolland and Møn.

Prices are set to rise by 0.7 percent on average across all transport types due to a yearly adjustment designed to cover the rising cost of running public transport, DOT said.

The rise will be most noticeable for commuters and pensioners, with the 2-7 zone commuter card rising by between 5 and 10 kroner, and the pensioner card rising by between 20 and 60 kroner depending on the type of card.

Those travelling on single tickets, or using the Rejsekort or Basiskort, will not be affected. (Ritzau)

Black Friday is just around the corner, and if you're planning on getting a good deal online this year, beware.
summary: Half of Denmark's drivers set to pay more for owning their vehicles next year, Black Friday shoppers warned to look out for scams and more news from Denmark on Tuesday.

title: Today in Italy: A roundup of the latest news on Tuesday
desc:
Italy set to receive record tourist tax revenue in 2026, more hoax bomb threats sent to Italian schools, and more news on Tuesday.

Italy is on course to make an unprecedented €1.3 billion from tourist taxes in 2026, up from €1.1 billion in 2025, SkyTG24 reported on Monday.

When Italy first allowed municipalities to levy a tax on overnight visitors in 2011, just 13 took advantage of the scheme, bringing in a total of €77 million.

Five regions accounted for 71 percent of earnings in 2025, according to the JFC Tourist Tax Observatory: Lazio, Rome’s region, took €300 million – 26.5 percent of the total – followed by Lombardy, Tuscany, Veneto and Trentino-Alto Adige.

The most significant increases in 2025 were recorded for Sardinia (+77.2 percent), Abruzzo (+53.5 percent), Friuli-Venezia Giulia (+48.9 percent), and Puglia (+42.9 percent).

Schools across Italy received more bomb threats on Monday following mass alerts that caused chaos last week, but very few evacuated after the government said they should be ignored.
summary: Italy set to receive record tourist tax revenue in 2026, more hoax bomb threats sent to Italian schools, and more news on Tuesday.

title: Today in Sweden: Centre-left set to open coalition talks with clashing demands
desc:
Sweden's centre-left parties are expected to begin their negotiations over forming a government this week – and markets see rising chance of Swedish interest rate hike before Christmas. Here's the latest news on Tuesday, November 17th.

Sweden's centre-left set to open coalition talks with clashing demands

Sweden's centre-left parties are set to begin their negotiations over forming a government this week, sources have told the TT news agency.

"Meetings are expected to pick up pace now. We aren't back at square one, when the Left Party refused to negotiate. We're in a better position now than before," a centrally placed Social Democrat source said.

The Centre Party on Sunday snubbed right-wing leader Ulf Kristersson in favour of Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson, and announced it was ready to sit down at the negotiating table.

"Our full focus now is to make this work and ensure it can become government policy," Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist said.

Left Party leader Nooshi Dadgostar met Andersson on Monday. She maintains that the Left Party is still sticking to its demand for ministerial posts, but welcomed the start of negotiations.
summary: Sweden's centre-left parties are expected to begin their negotiations over forming a government this week – and markets see rising chance of Swedish interest rate hike before Christmas. Here's the latest news on Tuesday, November 17th.
