title: How can you retrain as a kindergarten teacher in Vienna?
desc:
Vienna is expanding its kindergarten teacher training programmes as it struggles with staff shortages. If you're considering a career change, there are many routes into the profession, including some courses with financial support and a job offer at the end.

Vienna has opened a new training campus in 1210 Floridsdorf, which creates 200 new places for people preparing to work in the city's kindergartens.

The expansion comes as interest in early childhood education careers is rising sharply, with applications for training programmes up by 71 percent compared with the same period last year, according to the Vienna Employment Promotion Fund (waff) .

Some of these courses are designed for career changers and don't require previous experience in education. And some programmes can also provide financial support while you study.

As The Local previously reported , approximately 1,800 early childhood teaching positions were vacant across Vienna in August, including around 840 in municipal kindergartens.
summary: Vienna is expanding its kindergarten teacher training programmes as it struggles with staff shortages. If you're considering a career change, there are many routes into the profession, including some courses with financial support and a job offer at the end.

title: Norwegian expression of the day: takk for i dag
desc:
Today's expression of the day is a useful way to sign off at the end of a busy workday, and a handy one to build on for other farewells in Norway.

Takk for i dag literally translates to "thanks for today," and it serves as one of Norway’s most common ways to say goodbye after spending time together. Using it is appropriate in most contexts; after spending a nice day with friends, with colleagues, or to your teacher after a day at school.

You don't necessarily need to be thanking people for something specific, rather just acknowledging the time you spent together during the day.

The linguistic roots of the words trace back to Old Norse: þǫkk (gratitude/thanks) and í dag (literally "in day").

The phrase is part of a broader Scandinavian etiquette system built around pairing the words takk for ("thanks for") with a specific event or timeframe. Other examples include takk for matten ("thanks for the food") or takk for sist ("thanks for the last time we saw each other").

While the individual words are centuries old, takk for i dag became a standardised everyday farewell during the 19th century.
summary: Today's expression of the day is a useful way to sign off at the end of a busy workday, and a handy one to build on for other farewells in Norway.

title: How Brexit has added to Norway's skilled worker visa delays
desc:
The Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) has struggled with growing delays in processing skilled worker permits, and one main reason is Britons moving to Norway to work after Brexit.

At the end of October, the government proposed changes to the skilled worker permit rules after admitting the current system has serious problems that have put strain on resources and driven up waiting times.

To that end, the Ministry of Labour and Social Inclusion published a public consultation paper to gather feedback from social organisations and various stakeholders in Norway about the changes.

In its consultation document, the ministry explained that the main reasons for the proposal are that around 10 percent of cases have been identified as fraudulent, and that the system has been hit by bottlenecks and a big rise in applications for this type of permit across the country.

Authorities explicitly said that the number of applications has gone up sharply since 2021 after the United Kingdom left the EU and the European Economic Area (EEA).
summary: The Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) has struggled with growing delays in processing skilled worker permits, and one main reason is Britons moving to Norway to work after Brexit.

title: Danish word of the day: ej
desc:
Photo by Francesco Ungaro on Unsplash and Nicolas Raymond/FlickR

Today’s word of the day is one you’re likely to hear when Danes are expressing some sort of emotion.

Ej is a useful little word in Danish which has two different meanings.

The first is an alternative to ikke , the Danish word for ‘not’. Ej can technically be used interchangeably with ikke , although it is an archaic form and therefore has a slightly more poetic or literary sound to it. If you fully substituted ikke with ej people would probably consider it a bit odd.

The exception is in certain specific phrases where ej has stuck around. One of these is tro det eller ej (believe it or not), and another is vel gjorde jeg ej! (no I didn’t!)

You’ll also occasionally see it in official documents as a substitute for ikke . For example, internationals moving to Denmark from countries which do not have surnames are often recorded in Denmark’s population register as having the surname Ej Efternavn – literally ‘no surname’.

The second meaning, which is particularly common among young Danes, is as an exclamation before some sort of emotion.
summary: Today’s word of the day is one you’re likely to hear when Danes are expressing some sort of emotion.

title: OPINION: Foreign retirees in France deserve to know more about citizenship changes
desc:
France's interior minister appears to have quietly made it easier for foreign retirees to become French citizens, even though important questions remain. The Local's Emma Pearson asks why the minister isn't telling everyone about the move.

Changes that will make life harder for foreigners in France are more often than not announced with drumrolls, fanfare, press conferences and plenty of headlines.

Changes that will make life easier for foreigners in France, by contrast, seem to slip out unnoticed.

Just such a change has now been made , when Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced that tough new rules on French citizenship have been "adapted", so that foreign retirees are no longer barred from becoming French on the grounds that their income is comprised of a foreign pension.

In a letter, he writes: " les modalités d'examen des demandes de naturalisation des personnes retraitées ont été adaptées, afin de mieux tenir compte de la spécificité et de la diversité de leurs situations ." (The procedures for assessing applications for naturalisation from retired people have been adapted to take better account of the specific nature and diversity of their circumstances.)
summary: France's interior minister appears to have quietly made it easier for foreign retirees to become French citizens, even though important questions remain. The Local's Emma Pearson asks why the minister isn't telling everyone about the move.

title: German word of the day: Augenweide
desc:
Bored of calling everything schön or hübsch? If your idea of giving a compliment in German relies on just ‘beautiful’ or ‘pretty’, then it may be time to up your game.

An Augenweide is something that delights you visually. Literally, it means an “eye pasture” or “eye meadow” and is used to describe anything from a lovely landscape to an elegant building or a beautifully presented meal.

"A feast for the eyes" is probably the closest English equivalent, although "easy on the eye" sometimes works too.

It’s a feminine compound noun – die Augenweide – combining Augen (eyes) with Weide (pasture) and conjuring the wonderfully pastoral image of somewhere your eyes can graze.

The term goes back to Middle High German ougenweide . While Weide now usually means ‘pasture’, it once had a broader meaning incorporating ideas of nourishment or refreshment – not just a place where animals grazed, but something which fed and sustained.

There's a limit to how many times anyone can say schön or hübsch , and sometimes it just feels plain ridiculous to keep using the same one or two words for a house, the weather or somebody’s new curtains.
summary: Bored of calling everything schön or hübsch? If your idea of giving a compliment in German relies on just ‘beautiful’ or ‘pretty’, then it may be time to up your game.

title: Cancellations and delays expected on Danish trains for next two weeks
desc:
From Monday, there will be disruptions on Danish trains in multiple parts of the country for around two weeks, according to Tony Bispeskov, head of information at Danish railway company DSB.

He warned the Ritzau newswire that this mainly affects the Odense to Fredericia line, as well as multiple parts of Zealand.

Regional trains between Odense and Fredericia will be replaced by rail replacement buses in both directions, with intercity and intercity fast trains running with delays.

"We expect that the main route between Copenhagen, Funen and Fredericia will see around 15 minutes of extra travel time," Bispeskov said.

This is due to the fact that trains on this route need to run at slower speeds, 80 km/h instead of the usual 180.

Trains on the Copenhagen-Næstved line will only run between Køge Nord and Næstved, and the fast trains between Helsingør and Copenhagen will not run during rush hour.

According to Bispeskov, "the vast majority" of trains are running as normal, but he warned that they could be delayed nonetheless.
summary: From Monday, there will be disruptions on Danish trains in multiple parts of the country for around two weeks, according to Tony Bispeskov, head of information at Danish railway company DSB.

title: What time do Spanish people go to bed?
desc:
It’s a well-known fact that Spaniards stay up late, they shop late, they dine late and they go out to party late – so what time do they actually go to bed and how much sleep are they getting?

You know the drill, dinner around 9pm or 10pm and nightclubs not getting going until 2am.

It may seem like Spaniards survive on less sleep than many other Europeans because everything is so much later, but is this the case?

Data from DuckDik Sense wristband users, which recorded 36,727 nights between July and October 2026, reveals that in Spain the average bedtime is 12.30am.

That is a whole hour later than the Germans, who go to bed on average at 11.25pm.

It's only 8 minutes later than the Portuguese, who go to bed at 12.22am, but 26 minutes later than those in Italy who go to bed at 12.04am.

It’s also 33 minutes later than the French, who go to bed at 11.57pm.

Out of these countries, however, it’s the Spaniards that wake up the latest, one average at 8.10am, so does this mean that Spaniards actually get the same amount of sleep as other Europeans, but it’s simply shifted?
summary: It’s a well-known fact that Spaniards stay up late, they shop late, they dine late and they go out to party late – so what time do they actually go to bed and how much sleep are they getting?

title: Norway’s biggest bank DNB to raise card fees
desc:
Prices in Norway continue to rise, and some increases can easily go unnoticed. Customers at DNB should know that they will soon have to pay more simply to keep their bank card.

DNB, the largest bank in the country with around 2.4 million customers, has confirmed that the annual fee for a standard bank card will increase from 295 to 348 kroner per year, as announced in a letter sent to customers.

This represents an 18 percent price hike, which will take effect from January 1st, 2027.

"The annual price has been unchanged since 2020. Since then, it has become more expensive to offer and administer cards. Therefore, we are now adjusting the price," DNB wrote in its notice to customers.

The increase comes shortly after the partly state-owned bank reported a pre-tax profit of 12.5 billion kroner for the third quarter of this year, according to Norwegian newspaper Aftenposten.

In its letter, DNB also states that customers who do not wish to accept the higher fee can reject the change and end their card agreement before January by contacting the bank.
summary: Prices in Norway continue to rise, and some increases can easily go unnoticed. Customers at DNB should know that they will soon have to pay more simply to keep their bank card.

title: Why does winter still catch Norway off guard every year?
desc:
Every year, everyone knows that winter is coming and meteorologists always warn when snowfall is on the way, yet it still seems like the country is never quite ready for it.

As soon as the first heavy snowfall hits the country, especially in the big cities, the headlines are always the same: chaos in Oslo, chaos on the roads around Bergen, traffic accidents piling up, etc.

You might expect that in a country like Norway, where winter lasts for months and heavy snow is a normal part of daily life, everything would be set up to run smoothly. In reality, though, that is not what happens (or at least not what commuters experience).

Oslo was one of the places where delays, travel problems, and cancellations were felt the most during the snowfall on Thursday, November 12th.

Oslo’s public transport authority, Ruter, confirmed on its website that at the end of October, it had already held winter-preparedness meetings alongside bus operators and road maintenance crews. However, in practice, more than 65 percent of bus routes were cancelled and a high number of traffic accidents were recorded during the day.
summary: Every year, everyone knows that winter is coming and meteorologists always warn when snowfall is on the way, yet it still seems like the country is never quite ready for it.

title: Spanish PM seeks election boost as Brazil's Lula visits
desc:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva met leftist ally Pedro Sánchez in Madrid on Monday, with his recent election comeback offering encouragement to the Spanish leader ahead of a snap vote on November 29th.

Lula, 81, secured re-election in Brazil in October after overcoming conservative rival Flavio Bolsonaro, overturning a first-round deficit to win a closely fought run-off.

The result came despite opinion polls in the final days of the campaign pointing to a Bolsonaro victory.

Sánchez has repeatedly cited Lula's victory as evidence that he too can defy opinion polls putting him behind right-wing parties.

"It happened in Brazil. It has just happened in the United States. And it will happen soon in Spain," the Socialist said after the Democrats secured a landslide victory in the US midterm elections earlier this month.

Sánchez, 54, and Lula have developed close political ties in recent years and are among the most prominent figures of the international left.

The two leaders embraced and shook hands outside the Moncloa Palace, the Spanish government's headquarters, before heading inside for talks on Monday.
summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva met leftist ally Pedro Sánchez in Madrid on Monday, with his recent election comeback offering encouragement to the Spanish leader ahead of a snap vote on November 29th.

title: EU clears UniCredit takeover of Germany's Commerzbank
desc:
The EU on Monday approved the takeover of Germany's Commerzbank by Italian bank UniCredit's, as Europe seeks to reinforce the bloc's banking sector.

With the acquisition of Commerzbank, UniCredit plans to cement its status as a European heavyweight, a goal shared by the European Union.

The EU believes better integration of the bloc's banking sector will help it keep up with US lenders and boost its competitiveness.

The approval "is a good example of the kind of cross-border merger that can deliver positive scaling up of EU banks, improve their efficiency, and help them better compete internationally", EU competition chief Teresa Ribera said.

The European Commission, the EU's powerful competition regulator, approved the acquisition after determining the deal would not raise competition concerns.

"We want stronger European banks, and we want to achieve this while safeguarding competition and protecting consumers," Ribera said.

The EU this year announced plans to overhaul its rulebook on company mergers as Brussels seeks to forge what it calls "European champions".
summary: The EU on Monday approved the takeover of Germany's Commerzbank by Italian bank UniCredit's, as Europe seeks to reinforce the bloc's banking sector.

title: Social Democrats offer work permit overhaul in 135-point pitch to Centre Party
desc:
The Social Democrats have promised the Centre Party to scrap the restrictive work permit rules brought in by the Tidö government and bring an end to 'talent deportations' as part of a new 'strict but reasonable migration policy'.

The proposal was included in the 135-point comprehensive policy package from the Social Democrats, which was obtained by public broadcaster SVT shortly after the Centre Party announced that it had chosen the left-wing parties ' "total package" of policy proposals over that of the right-wing Moderate Party. The Social Democrats promised the policies would be carried out in a coalition excluding the Left Party.

According to reports in SVT and Dagens Nyheter (and to The Local's sources within the parties), both the Social Democrats and the Moderate Party proposed policies which would soften the impact of the "paradigm shift on migration" carried out over the past four years.

The Social Democrats' proposed new work permit regime would have a lower salary threshold, and would also be more flexible, allowing businesses and public health and welfare organisations to more easily recruit the staff they need internationally.
summary: The Social Democrats have promised the Centre Party to scrap the restrictive work permit rules brought in by the Tidö government and bring an end to 'talent deportations' as part of a new 'strict but reasonable migration policy'.

title: What is the average salary in Denmark and which sectors pay best?
desc:
Denmark is known to have a labour market that generally pays well, helping to offset the country’s high prices. What can you expect to earn on average, and how do salaries vary according to sector and location? We take a look at the stats.

The average monthly salary for someone working full-time in Denmark’s labour market is 53,916 kroner according to the most recent figure from national agency Statistics Denmark , based on data from 2025.

The median salary was 48,700 kroner, with an average salary of 56,053 kroner in the private sector and 56,053 kroner in the public sector.

The monthly wage calculation includes bonuses and pension contributions but not overtime.

Breaking average wage statistics down into different regions, employees in the Capital Region were in general paid more than those in other regions, across all sectors.

Those paid least were in the North Jutland region, where those working for the state were paid 50,306 kroner on average, those working for the region were paid 51,889 kroner on average and those in the private sector were paid an average of 50,295 kroner per month.
summary: Denmark is known to have a labour market that generally pays well, helping to offset the country’s high prices. What can you expect to earn on average, and how do salaries vary according to sector and location? We take a look at the stats.

title: Paris court imposes €110,000 fine for illegal Airbnb rental
desc:
A Paris landlord has been ordered to pay €110,000 for illegally renting out an apartment on Airbnb under France's tough new law on holiday rentals.

The ruling by the Paris District Court marks the first time a court has imposed the maximum €100,000 penalty for this type of offence, according to Paris City Hall. In this case, the court also imposed an additional €10,000 fine on the landlord for failing to provide rental records requested by the City of Paris.

It comes under France's anti-Airbnb’ law, also known as the Echaniz-Le Meur Act, which came into force on November 19th, 2024. The legislation, named after the two MPs who drafted it, strengthened local authorities' powers to regulate short-term holiday rentals and increased the penalties for landlords who break the rules.

According to the court ruling , the 63-square-metre apartment in the 8th arrondissement of Paris was rented out for 351 nights in 2025 and a further 202 nights between January and July 2026, based on Airbnb records alone.
summary: A Paris landlord has been ordered to pay €110,000 for illegally renting out an apartment on Airbnb under France's tough new law on holiday rentals.

title: Surviving Danish Christmas: How to decorate like a Dane
desc:
It's that time of year when cities across Denmark are decked out in lights, garlands and other beautiful (and sometimes garish) decorations. If you want to decorate your home like a Dane, or maybe host a Christmas craft event, keep reading.

You may have spotted candles at your local supermarket with numbers down the side, allowing you to burn down a number for each day of December until Christmas. This in Danish is known as a kalenderlys . You can put it in a candle holder and simply light the candle every day, or you can make a juledekoration with your kalenderlys .

This typically involves a big lump of clay pressed into a plate, pine branches, and Christmas decorations. The world is your oyster when it comes to how to assemble the decoration, but traditionally the candle is pushed into the centre of the clay-lined plate, with the pine branches and decorations surrounding it.

Beware that if you use this for the whole Christmas season the leaves and pine needles may dry out, so make sure not to leave the candle unattended.
summary: It's that time of year when cities across Denmark are decked out in lights, garlands and other beautiful (and sometimes garish) decorations. If you want to decorate your home like a Dane, or maybe host a Christmas craft event, keep reading.

title: Revolut Italy placed under supervision over money laundering checks
desc:
An Italian court has placed the Italian branch of British digital bank Revolut under external supervision because of insufficient money laundering checks, according to a court document seen by AFP on Monday.

The Milan court document dated November 12 said several people under investigation for suspected mafia links had been able to use the bank -- without its knowledge -- to commit money laundering and tax fraud.

The court said it found that at least 24 clients who were under investigation had funnelled or hidden funds amounting to around 41.9 million euros ($46.1 million) through the bank between 2021 and 2026.

Revolut said that it would "cooperate fully" with Italian authorities and that its banking services in Italy "would continue to operate normally".

"We take our regulatory obligations and anti-money laundering controls extremely seriously, and we continuously invest in strengthening our financial crime systems, transaction monitoring models, and dedicated compliance teams across all markets," the bank said in a statement.
summary: An Italian court has placed the Italian branch of British digital bank Revolut under external supervision because of insufficient money laundering checks, according to a court document seen by AFP on Monday.

title: TELL US: Is Switzerland still affordable or has it become too expensive to live here?
desc:
Survey data shows that people living in Switzerland increasingly worry about the cost of living. The Local wants your thoughts, as well as any tips or tricks to cut costs.

Is Switzerland still affordable or has it become too expensive to live? The Local wants to know what you think.

A recent survey carried out by WTW consulting firm, 38 percent of respondents in Switzerland stated that they face financial issues that negatively affect their lives - up from 25 percent the previous year.

But that's not all: nearly half (49 percent) expect to find themselves in a less favourable financial situation in retirement than their parents' generation.

Is the situation just as bad for foreign residents In Switzerland?

The Local is therefore looking for insight from our readers on what they think and how they save on living costs in Switzerland.

You can fill out the short survey via the link HERE or below.

Join the conversation in our comments section below. Share your own views and experience and if you have a question or suggestion for our journalists then email us at news@thelocal.ch . Please keep comments civil, constructive and on topic – and make sure to read our terms of use before getting involved.
summary: Survey data shows that people living in Switzerland increasingly worry about the cost of living. The Local wants your thoughts, as well as any tips or tricks to cut costs.

title: On the Agenda: What's happening in Italy this week
desc:
A national general strike impacting travel and renewed student protests coming up this weekend.

Drivers on Italian roads must now have winter tyres fitted or snow chains on board, from Sunday until April 15th.

There’s no single national list: each region sets its own rules , covering stretches of motorway as well as provincial roads in areas such as Como, Pavia, Rimini and Cuneo. All-season tyres marked M+S are also covered by the rules.

Tuesday is the deadline for parliamentary amendments to the 2027 budget, after a week of hearings in the lower house’s budget committee on the €26 billion plan.

The headline tax change extends the 33 percent income tax rate to incomes of up to €55,000, from €50,000.

Parliament has until the end of December to approve the final text.

Statistics office Istat is due on Tuesday to publish final figures for October, after its preliminary estimate showed inflation jumping to 5.4 percent from 4.2 percent in September, the highest level since August 2023.

Energy was the main driver, up 31.4 percent on a year earlier. Prices have been climbing all autumn: September’s figure was already a three-year high , and consumer groups warned of hundreds of euros in extra utility costs this year.
summary: A national general strike impacting travel and renewed student protests coming up this weekend.

title: Italy a 'key hotspot' for climate crisis with extreme weather on the rise
desc:
Environmental groups have urged Italy to fund its stalled climate plan in the 2027 budget as the number of extreme weather events rose dramatically in the past decade.

Extreme weather killed at least 221 people in Italy between 2015 and September 2026, environmental organisation Legambiente said on Friday as the UN’s COP31 climate summit in Antalya got underway.

The climate crisis cost Italy an estimated €147 billion in financial damages from 1980 to 2026, making it the European country that has suffered the worst economic losses, according to Legambiente’s 2026 Città Clima report , produced with insurance group Unipol.

“Italy's geographical location is particularly delicate because it is at the centre of the Mediterranean basin, recognised by the scientific community as one of the main global climate change hotspots”, said Legambiente geographer Gabriele Nanni.

The climate crisis has struck the north particularly hard, with 1,237 extreme weather events recorded since 2015, followed by the south (827) and central Italy (625). On a regional level, Lombardy is the most exposed, followed by Emilia Romagna and Sicily.
summary: Environmental groups have urged Italy to fund its stalled climate plan in the 2027 budget as the number of extreme weather events rose dramatically in the past decade.

title: What travellers need to know about Lufthansa's new check-in rule
desc:
Your booking code and surname alone are no longer enough to get you a boarding pass on certain Lufthansa Group flights. Here's who needs a free Travel ID account and from which airports.

If you check in online for Lufthansa, Swiss, Austrian or other Lufthansa Group flights, a booking code and surname might no longer be enough. You'll also need a free user account called a Travel ID.

Many frequent flyers will probably have an account already, so the change is more likely to affect occasional flyers.

The rule, which is being phased in by departure airport, reached Munich on Monday and will affect travellers from Frankfurt from November 30th.

Until now, the routine was simple. You got the "check-in is open" email, clicked the link, typed in your booking code and surname, and your boarding pass appeared.

The rollout started on October 20th and is being introduced in stages:

October 20th: Schengen-area airports, excluding Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

November 2nd: European countries outside Schengen, plus airports in Germany (except Frankfurt and Munich), Austria and Switzerland (except Zurich).
summary: Your booking code and surname alone are no longer enough to get you a boarding pass on certain Lufthansa Group flights. Here's who needs a free Travel ID account and from which airports.

title: EU 'breakthrough' to allow streamlined checks at UK-France border
desc:
The operators of Eurotunnel say they have achieved a 'breakthrough' deal with the EU to allow airport-style checks to prevent travel chaos with the full implementation of EES passport controls at Folkestone and Calais.

The departure points of Le Shuttle at Folkestone and Calais are among several on the UK-France border where the new EES passport checks have still not been fully implemented because of fears of travel chaos.

Despite the EU's new Entry & Exit System officially coming into full effect in April 2026, France has not fully rolled it out at key crossing points including the Eurostar, Port of Dover and Eurotunnel because of technical faults and the fears of long delays.

However, this week Yann Leriche, CEO of Getlink, which owns the Channel Tunnel, announced a 'breakthrough' deal with the EU to use an airport-style camera system at Le Shuttle's departure points, to avoid drivers having to get out of their cars to complete the fingerprinting and facial scans that are necessary for EES registration.
summary: The operators of Eurotunnel say they have achieved a 'breakthrough' deal with the EU to allow airport-style checks to prevent travel chaos with the full implementation of EES passport controls at Folkestone and Calais.

title: French Expression of the Day: Se gourer
desc:
Often heard in conversation, this French expression is quite informal but can be used in everyday situations.

A good French expression to know if you've made a small mistake.

The expression se gourer , roughly pronounced suh gou-ray (listen here ), means "to be wrong", "to make a mistake" or "to get something wrong".

It is a very common and informal French expression - you'll hear it in everyday conversations when someone made a mistake, got the wrong idea or confused something. It can refer to small, everyday mistakes, such as getting an address, date or name wrong, but it isn't limited to minor errors. You can also use it for bigger misunderstandings or being completely mistaken about something.

It is similar to se tromper , which also means to make a mistake, but se gourer is more colloquial. Due to its informal form, it is best to use it with family and friends rather than in professional situations.

The exact origins of se gourer are uncertain, and several theories exist. According to the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française, one possibility is that it comes from the Arabic word gurur , meaning deception or illusion, which may have entered French via the Spanish verb engorrar , meaning to embarrass or annoy.
summary: Often heard in conversation, this French expression is quite informal but can be used in everyday situations.

title: Austria sees hike in number of people granted citizenship in 2026
desc:
Nearly 20,000 people became Austrian in the first three quarters of 2026 – a 13 percent rise compared to the same period last year.

A total of 19,930 people received Austrian citizenship from the beginning of the year up until the end of September, official figures show. Of this group, 14,171 were resident in Austria, while 5,759 lived abroad.

Manuela Lenk, Director General at Statistics Austria, said most of the naturalisations were granted "on the basis of at least six years’ residence in Austria and on grounds warranting special consideration".

Lenk added that this group had "grown significantly" compared with the first three quarters of the previous year. Meanwhile, the number of naturalisations of people living abroad has fallen.

To naturalise in Austria, people generally need to have lived in the country legally for 10 years (and had a permanent residence permit for at least five years). However, people who meet certain requirements – such as having strong German language skills and being well-integrated – can apply after six years.
summary: Nearly 20,000 people became Austrian in the first three quarters of 2026 – a 13 percent rise compared to the same period last year.

title: Further rail strikes in Spain called for Tuesday November 17th
desc:
A new round of strikes will hit Spanish trains on Tuesday. Here's what you need to know about which trains will be affected and what minimum services have been established.

The Spanish Union of Train Drivers and Railway Assistants (Semaf), the Workers' Commissions (CCOO), General Union of Workers (UGT) and other railway unions have called for another walkout this month, following October's deadly Urda train collision, to demand greater safety, staffing, and public rail guarantees.

The 24-hour strike is due to take place on Tuesday November 17th starting at midnight on Monday, and will affect all rail services throughout Spain, including commuter and medium-distance, long-distance and high-speed services.

Adif infrastructure staff, as well as private high-speed operators Iryo and Ouigo will also be taking part.

According to a statement released by Renfe, minimum services will be established.

On the Cercanías commuter rail network during peak hours (6-9am 1.30-3.30pm and 18.30pm to 20.30pm), 75 percent of the usual service will be running. During the rest of the day, 50 percent of trains are scheduled to run.
summary: A new round of strikes will hit Spanish trains on Tuesday. Here's what you need to know about which trains will be affected and what minimum services have been established.

title: What are the new SWISS and Edelweiss check-in rules?
desc:
Travellers leaving Swiss airports on Lufthansa group airlines should known about the new change to check-in requirements.

Travellers using SWISS and Edelweiss airlines now require a 'Travel ID' for online check-in.

From November 16th, the policy change applies to flights departing from Zurich, but will be extended to other regions by the end of November.

It will become mandatory for checking in for flights online, but will not be required for passengers using a self-service kiosk or a counter at the airport.

According to information from SWISS : "Travel ID makes your travels even easier. It’s your login for all our digital services. It lets you access your data quickly and easily, and you benefit from relevant information and personalised services at all times."

The new requirement comes from parent company Lufthansa and also applies to Edelweiss.

Anyone who does not yet have such an account will need to register before travelling, besides in a few special cases.

Anyone who does not wish to have a Travel-ID can still check in at the counter or using a self-service kiosk.
summary: Travellers leaving Swiss airports on Lufthansa group airlines should known about the new change to check-in requirements.

title: German city scraps 'wolf in sheep's clothing' posters after Muslim community anger
desc:
Local authorities in the German city of Bremen have ended a security-awareness campaign just ten days after it began, admitting that the image it chose cast general suspicion on Muslims.

Bremen has pulled a poster campaign showing a wolf in sheep's clothing after complaints from the Muslim community.

The city's interior senator Eva Högl (SPD) admitted that it cast suspicion on many people who were never its target. "I deeply regret this," she said .

Högl added that: "The goal was right. The implementation was not."

But critics, including the news site Migazin, argue that the problem wasn't only the design, but also the idea behind it.

Bremen’s Interior Department announced a partnership with the outdoor advertising company Ströer in April this year.

Under the agreement, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) in Bremen was to use digital advertising spaces to warn the public about dangers.

The BfV is Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. The agreement with Ströer is reportedly the first collaboration of its kind in the country.
summary: Local authorities in the German city of Bremen have ended a security-awareness campaign just ten days after it began, admitting that the image it chose cast general suspicion on Muslims.

title: REVEALED: The undisputed best French cheese (sort of)
desc:
The Local can exclusively reveal which French cheese has been officially crowned the best (according to a poll of our readers).

France has a lot* of cheeses. In fact, it can be hard to decide which one to add to your after-dinner cheeseboard.

So we decided to ask our readers which they regard as the best fromage of all - not only did they have to name the cheese that they considered the best, they had to make the case for why it is superior to the roughly 999* other French cheeses available.

Dozens of Local readers bravely took on this task, and their lyrical descriptions and attention to detail proved that they had truly understood the assignment.

Andy Wood, from Holywood, Northern Ireland, nominated époisses, praising its: "Variety of tastes and textures - tangy to creamy, salty to milky and spreadability/spoonability - all things to all cheese lovers."

Jill Brown, in Geneva, voted for comté, saying: "It is perfect for eating alone, for making a croque monsieur/ madame , grating onto pasta, putting into quiche or a sandwich, it is so versatile and the older the better."
summary: The Local can exclusively reveal which French cheese has been officially crowned the best (according to a poll of our readers).

title: Minister announces 'adaptation' of rules on French citizenship
desc:
France's Interior Minister says that some of the tougher new rules on acquiring French citizenship have been adapted, although questions remain about what this means for foreigners in France.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez says that tough new rules on French citizenship have been "adapted" to take into account the situation of foreign retirees in France.

In a letter, Nunez says: " les modalités d'examen des demandes de naturalisation des personnes retraitées ont été adaptées, afin de mieux tenir compte de la spécificité et de la diversité de leurs situations ." (The procedures for assessing applications for naturalisation from retired people have been adapted to take better account of the specific nature and diversity of their circumstances.)

The comment was made in a letter to Charente senator Nicole Bonnefoy, who has repeatedly highlighted the impact of tough new income requirements for citizenship on foreign retirees.

Since May 2025, préfectures have been instructed that only "French-sourced" income can be taken into account when assessing the financial situation of people applying for French citizenship by residency ( par décret ).
summary: France's Interior Minister says that some of the tougher new rules on acquiring French citizenship have been adapted, although questions remain about what this means for foreigners in France.

title: What happens next in negotiations for Sweden's next PM?
desc:
It's 64 days since Sweden's general election and the auction the Centre Party launched ten days ago has not yielded a clear prime ministerial candidate. So are we back to square one? Here's what happens next in the process of choosing Sweden's next PM.

Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist announced on Sunday night that her party had chosen the "total package" submitted by Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson over that of her Moderate rival Ulf Kristersson.

That is not as decisive as it might seem: Andersson's proposed package was based around a government without ministers from the Left Party; Thand Ringqvist said that it was this that her party had chosen, stressing that the Centre Party would still refuse to back a government that includes Left Party ministers. Left Party deputy leader Ida Gabrielsson shortly afterwards went out on public broadcaster SVT and said that her party's demand for a ministerial position remained in place.

So the deadlock remains in place. But the parties are not necessarily back where they started. If reports in Expressen and other newspapers are correct, Thand Ringqvist had wanted to choose Kristersson's package. If this is true, then it seems she didn't get her party's backing.
summary: It's 64 days since Sweden's general election and the auction the Centre Party launched ten days ago has not yielded a clear prime ministerial candidate. So are we back to square one? Here's what happens next in the process of choosing Sweden's next PM.

title: When will Switzerland's referendum on EU treaties take place?
desc:
A packed legislative session means that the referendum to vote on updated treaties outlining Switzerland's relationship with the EU could be pushed back even further.

The referendum on a new batch of agreements between Bern and Brussels outlining Switzerland's relationship with the EU will be further delayed, reports in the Swiss media suggest.

In September MPs debated the details of the bilateral treaties , known as Bilaterals III, which are awaiting ratification, working under the impression that the agreements would be put to a referendum in 2027.

A packed legislative session to end the year, however, means that this will likely not happen until 2028 at the earliest .

This is also due to unresolved issues between the Council of states and National Council regarding the modalities of the vote itself, namely whether it should be put to a mandatory or optional referendum.

The National Council intends to debate the treaty package from start to finish during the winter session and is planning extra sitting hours to do so, according to reports from Swiss public broadcaster SRF.
summary: A packed legislative session means that the referendum to vote on updated treaties outlining Switzerland's relationship with the EU could be pushed back even further.

title: Left Party stands firm on cabinet demand after Centre Party backs red-green bloc
desc:
The Centre Party has snubbed Moderate leader Ulf Kristersson in favour of Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson. But as far as negotiations are going, it's back to square one.

Left Party deputy leader Ida Gabrielsson welcomed the Centre Party's decision to move forward with a centre-left, "red-green", government alternative.

"Forming a government is too important for us to hold grudges. Now we have to go back to square one," the TT news agency quoted her as saying.

She said her party was "of course ready to negotiate" but stressed that they're still holding firm to their demand for cabinet seats.

"We haven't changed our position, and Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist knows that full well," she said of the Centre Party leader.

Earlier on Sunday, Thand Ringqvist announced that her party had opted to move forward with the policy package presented by Social Democrat leader Andersson, while simultaneously ruling out the Left Party joining the cabinet. Asked how the Left Party plans to act given that the Centre Party continues to say no to them sitting in government, Gabrielsson responded that no party can get all of its demands met.
summary: The Centre Party has snubbed Moderate leader Ulf Kristersson in favour of Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson. But as far as negotiations are going, it's back to square one.

title: MAPS: What to expect from France's November 17th strikes and protests
desc:
Public sector workers in France will be staging a second one-day strike after talks between unions and the government on public sector pay ended without agreement. Here's what to expect on Tuesday.

Unions representing public sector workers have called a one-day strike on Tuesday, November 17th, following a similar one-day action on November 5th.

The strike call was made by the intersyndicale for public sector workers, which represents all public sector unions. It has since been joined by rail workers' unions, students and lycée pupils.

They are calling for pay increases for public sector workers so that salaries better reflect the rising cost of living - a meeting between unions and the prime minister last week ended without agreement.

The November 5th strike did not cause widespread disruption, and at present it looks like November 17th will be similar.

Trains - on the railways, the CGT, SUD-Rail and CFDT unions have filed strike notices, meaning there could be some disruption. SNCF will publish a detailed strike timetable on Monday evening, and anyone who has booked onto a train that is cancelled will be notified directly.
summary: Public sector workers in France will be staging a second one-day strike after talks between unions and the government on public sector pay ended without agreement. Here's what to expect on Tuesday.

title: Five EU countries set to unveil Rwanda 'return hub' deal
desc:
Five EU countries including Germany, Austria and Denmark were set to announce a deal to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda on Monday – the first such facility outside the bloc, with the EU welcoming the initiative.

The group, also comprising Greece and the Netherlands, has been gunning to open a "return-hub" despite rights groups' concerns, after the European Union cleared the way with a recent toughening of migration rules.

The five have kept the location under wraps as they negotiated with potential hosts, but European diplomats and other people briefed on the talks have indicated Rwanda as the chosen country.

The African nation had confirmed in August it had begun "preliminary discussions" with several European states.

It is sending a delegation to a migration conference in Vienna, where several sources said the agreement would be unveiled at a press conference on Monday.

Ministers from the five EU countries gathered in the interior ministry in Vienna from 2:30 pm local time (1330 GMT) for a "working session".
summary: Five EU countries including Germany, Austria and Denmark were set to announce a deal to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda on Monday – the first such facility outside the bloc, with the EU welcoming the initiative.

title: Paying by invoice in Sweden? Expect more personal questions from Klarna
desc:
A new law may make you have to reveal more personal details to the likes of Klarna and Qliro.

Sweden's new Consumer Credit Act will come into force on November 20th, a change that may have passed many people by unnoticed – unless you've used payment services like Klarna lately.

In its app, among other places, Klarna has started asking customers to fill in details about their personal finances and living situation so that the company can "assess what you can afford", as it writes.

"Credit providers are obligated to ask more questions and collect more types of information. It must be a thorough check, as it is now phrased. Previously, it could be done more at their own discretion," Anna Lindström, a lawyer at the Swedish Consumer Agency, told the TT newswire.

The new law, which was passed in January 2026, means that more types of credit are covered by the rules, including interest-free credit provided by third parties, such as Klarna or similar companies. It's intended to crack down on over-indebtedness. The information customers could be asked to provide could include annual income, number of children and type of employment.
summary: A new law may make you have to reveal more personal details to the likes of Klarna and Qliro.

title: Today in Denmark: A roundup of the latest news on Monday
desc:
Denmark expected to unveil 'departure centre' deal with Rwanda, cancellations and delays on Danish trains for next two weeks and more news from Denmark on Monday.

It looks like things will be rainy and windy for most of this week, with rain forecast on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.

On Thursday and Friday temperatures will drop to between 6 degrees and freezing, which means there could be some snow (or more likely, slush) in store, according to Sandra Nygaard, on-duty meteorologist at Danish weather agency DMI.

"It could start to get a bit wintry on Thursday and Friday, with frost at night," she said, adding that at the moment it looks like this will mainly affect southern and eastern Denmark, although the forecast is still uncertain.

As far as the weekend is concerned, the forecast so far is dry, although this could change.

Cancellations and delays expected on Danish trains for next two weeks

Starting on Monday morning, there will be disruptions on the Danish trains in multiple parts of the country for around two weeks, according to Tony Bispeskov, head of information at Danish railway company DSB.
summary: Denmark expected to unveil 'departure centre' deal with Rwanda, cancellations and delays on Danish trains for next two weeks and more news from Denmark on Monday.

title: Climate takes back seat in Spain election despite flood, fires
desc:
Maria Laura Bustamante had barely finished furnishing the home she had just bought with her husband in the Spanish town of Paiporta when floods swept through the area, destroying the flat.

The disaster also destroyed the Latin Grammy-nominated couple's home recording studio, where Bustamante and her husband, Alejandro Rivas, professional musicians who perform together, worked on their music.

Spain's deadliest floods in a generation devastated the eastern region of Valencia in October 2024, sweeping away cars, submerging roads and buildings, cutting off residents and claiming more than 230 lives.

The couple and their young daughter spent the following months living in the nearby city of Valencia while their flat was being repaired.

"I used to find it difficult to imagine that climate change could affect us or force us to leave our homes," Bustamante, 40, told AFP on the terrace of her home in Paiporta, one of the hardest-hit towns. "It seemed a long way off."

The experience inspired the couple to write " El rio no tiene culpa " (The River Is Not to Blame), a song reflecting on climate change and criticising the authorities' handling of the floods.
summary: Maria Laura Bustamante had barely finished furnishing the home she had just bought with her husband in the Spanish town of Paiporta when floods swept through the area, destroying the flat.

title: Today in Spain: A roundup of the latest news on Monday
desc:
England beat Spain in Nations League to end record unbeaten run, housing encampment in Barcelona finally dismantled, Canary Islands break record for daily rescues, and more news from Spain this Monday November 16th.

England beat Spain in Nations League to end record unbeaten run

England snapped world champions Spain's record unbeaten run with a 3-2 victory in Madrid on Sunday to clinch the top spot in Nations League group A3.

Goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White inflicted La Roja's first loss in a competitive game since March 2023, after 44 without defeat.

England's Elliot Anderson was sent off in the second half as Spain fought back from three goals down with strikes from Mikel Oyarzabal and Nico Williams, but Luis de la Fuente's World Cup winners could not find the equaliser.

Both sides were already sure to progress, but as group winners England will be seeded for the quarter-finals in March.

Spain had beaten England in the Euro 2024 final before adding a second world crown this summer, while the Three Lions finished third.
summary: England beat Spain in Nations League to end record unbeaten run, housing encampment in Barcelona finally dismantled, Canary Islands break record for daily rescues, and more news from Spain this Monday November 16th.

title: Today in Switzerland: A roundup of the latest news on Monday
desc:
Vote on EU treaty package is not likely until 2028 at the earliest; Switzerland to face stormy winds over the coming days; and more news in our Monday roundup.

Vote on EU treaty package is not likely until 2028 at the earliest

The new batch of agreements between Bern and Brussels - the so-called Bilaterals III - will not go into effect until ratified, which will take longer than initially thought.

Intended to go to a referendum in 2027, it now seems likely that this will not happen until 2028 at the earliest , due to still-unresolved issues between the Council of states and the National Council regarding the modalities of the vote itself - that is, whether it should put to a mandatory or optional referendum.

The National Council must still weigh in on this issue before the final date - sometime in 2028 - can be set.

Brace yourself: Switzerland to face stormy winds over the coming days

After a relatively calm weekend, strong gusts will sweep across Switzerland from today, blowing with sometimes gale-force intensity for the next several days. Al the regions will be affected, according to forecasts from MeteoSchweiz weather service.
summary: Vote on EU treaty package is not likely until 2028 at the earliest; Switzerland to face stormy winds over the coming days; and more news in our Monday roundup.

title: Police ban protests near some Paris schools and universities
desc:
The police in Paris on Sunday issued a ban on protests near 10 lycées and five universities, amid a blockade movement that has gone on for two months.

The order prohibits unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100 metres of the sites from Monday through to Friday.

Lycée pupils aged between 15 and 18 began to blockade school entrances in mid-September to protest against substandard classroom conditions.

University students joined the movement, which quickly spread around France and fed into other demonstrations by unions over inflation and the cost of living.

The police ban applies to 10 of the French capital's roughly 150 secondary schools, and to universities including faculties at the Sorbonne.

Paris police chief Patrice Faure said in the order that the ban was necessary because of "numerous disruptions and blockades around certain lycées and establishments of higher learning in Paris and the surrounding region, as part of a social movement at persistent scale and violence".

He said 1,548 arrests had been made since the start of the protests and several public buildings vandalised.
summary: The police in Paris on Sunday issued a ban on protests near 10 lycées and five universities, amid a blockade movement that has gone on for two months.

title: Today in Sweden: Left Party says government negotiations are 'back to square one'
desc:
Sweden's Left Party stands firm on cabinet demand after Centre Party backs red-green bloc – and a new law may make you have to reveal more personal details to the likes of Klarna. Here's the latest news on Monday, November 16th.

Left Party stands firm on cabinet demand after Centre Party backs red-green bloc

Left Party deputy leader Ida Gabrielsson welcomed the Centre Party's decision to move forward with a centre-left, "red-green", government alternative.

"Forming a government is too important for us to hold grudges. Now we have to go back to square one," the TT news agency quoted her as saying.

She said her party was "of course ready to negotiate" but stressed that they're still holding firm to their demand for cabinet seats.

"We haven't changed our position, and Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist knows that full well," she said of the Centre Party leader.

Earlier on Sunday, Thand Ringqvist announced that her party had opted to move forward with the policy package presented by Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson, while simultaneously ruling out the Left Party joining the cabinet.
summary: Sweden's Left Party stands firm on cabinet demand after Centre Party backs red-green bloc – and a new law may make you have to reveal more personal details to the likes of Klarna. Here's the latest news on Monday, November 16th.

title: Today in Italy: A roundup of the latest news on Monday
desc:
Bolzano named Italy’s ‘best’ place to live in 2026, more unstable weather forecast across Italy, and more news on Monday.

Bolzano is the Italian province with the best quality of life in 2026, displacing Milan from the top spot, according to the latest edition of a popular ranking.

Italia Oggi and La Sapienza’s Qualità della Vita ranking grades the country’s 107 provinces based on nine factors, including 'business and work' – which measures employment rates – healthcare, environment, education, crime and culture.

Bolzano scored particularly highly for its performance in the areas of work, environmental quality and culture. Milan ranked second overall for 2026, while Bologna came in third.

The survey reveals a stark north-south divide, with all 22 of the provinces in the northeast deemed to provide a ‘good’ or ‘acceptable’ quality of life. The 21 lowest-scoring provinces were located in the south or major islands, with Puglia’s Taranto coming in last.

Italy is set to be hit by more severe weather following a brief respite over the weekend, forecasters warned, with strong winds and heavy rain expected from Monday.
summary: Bolzano named Italy’s ‘best’ place to live in 2026, more unstable weather forecast across Italy, and more news on Monday.

title: Swedish electricity prices set to spike after Forsmark 3 nuclear reactor halts
desc:
Sweden's Forsmark 3 nuclear reactor has had to shut down due to a short circuit, which is expected to send electricity prices soaring even further.

Forsmark 3's shutdown means that four of Sweden's six reactors are currently out of action.

According to energy market analyst Christian Holtz from Polite Energy, the halt means both lower electricity production in southern Sweden and potential difficulties in transmitting power from north to south.

"That creates a double effect in southern Sweden, and it could add several tens of öre per kilowatt-hour, particularly in the middle and end of [this] week, Thursday to Friday, as it will turn a bit colder and possibly also a bit less windy," Holtz told TT.

High gas prices driving up electricity costs on the continent alongside low water levels in reservoirs – particularly in southern Norway – are also contributing to the effect.

Holtz advises households to first and foremost reduce their overall electricity consumption.

"Right now, price levels are fairly high during all hours or quarter-hours. However, this coming Thursday and Friday, they will definitely spike extra sharply in the morning. If you can be flexible with your usage and also have a quarter-hourly electricity contract, there's quite a bit of money to be saved," he said.
summary: Sweden's Forsmark 3 nuclear reactor has had to shut down due to a short circuit, which is expected to send electricity prices soaring even further.

title: Sweden's Centre Party picks Social Democrats in government negotiations
desc:
Sweden's Centre Party has chosen to continue negotiating with the centre-left parties in the hope of forming a government, party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist announced late on Sunday.

On Friday, the Centre Party received what it has referred to as "total packages" – containing policy proposals and an outline of how they would be implemented – from Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson on the left and Moderate leader Ulf Kristersson on the right.

Thand Ringqvist described their proposals as "serious and thorough".

"After reviewing Andersson's total package, our decision is that the Social Democrats' alternative is the one we are choosing to negotiate further on," she told the TT news agency in a written statement.

However, there's still the issue of the Left Party's demand for ministerial posts in a centre-left government.

"Several crucial questions remain regarding the content and direction of the policies, the financing of key reforms, and parliamentary support. This requires the Left Party to drop its demand to be part of the government, and for them and the Green Party to back the proposed total package," Thand Ringqvist wrote.
summary: Sweden's Centre Party has chosen to continue negotiating with the centre-left parties in the hope of forming a government, party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist announced late on Sunday.
titleTh: พรรคกลางของสวีเดนเลือกพรรคโซเชียลเดโมแครตในการเจรจากับรัฐบาล
descTh:
พรรคกลางของสวีเดนเลือกที่จะเจรจากับพรรคกลางซ้ายต่อไปด้วยความหวังว่าจะจัดตั้งรัฐบาล หัวหน้าพรรค อลิซาเบธ ทันด์ ริงควิสต์ ประกาศเมื่อวันอาทิตย์ที่ผ่านมา

เมื่อวันศุกร์ พรรคกลางได้รับสิ่งที่เรียกว่า "แพ็คเกจรวม" ซึ่งประกอบด้วยข้อเสนอนโยบายและโครงร่างวิธีการนำไปปฏิบัติ จากผู้นำพรรคโซเชียลเดโมแครต แม็กดาเลนา แอนเดอร์สสันทางซ้าย และผู้นำระดับปานกลาง อุล์ฟ คริสเตอร์สันทางขวา

Thand Ringqvist กล่าวถึงข้อเสนอของพวกเขาว่า "จริงจังและถี่ถ้วน"

“หลังจากตรวจสอบแผนทั้งหมดของแอนเดอร์สสันแล้ว การตัดสินใจของเราก็คือทางเลือกของพรรคโซเชียลเดโมแครตคือทางเลือกที่เราเลือกที่จะเจรจาต่อไป” เธอบอกกับสำนักข่าว TT ในแถลงการณ์ที่เป็นลายลักษณ์อักษร

อย่างไรก็ตาม ยังคงมีปัญหาข้อเรียกร้องของพรรคฝ่ายซ้ายให้ดำรงตำแหน่งรัฐมนตรีในรัฐบาลกลางซ้าย

“คำถามสำคัญหลายประการยังคงอยู่เกี่ยวกับเนื้อหาและทิศทางของนโยบาย การจัดหาเงินทุนสำหรับการปฏิรูปที่สำคัญ และการสนับสนุนจากรัฐสภา สิ่งนี้ทำให้พรรคฝ่ายซ้ายต้องยกเลิกการเรียกร้องที่จะเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของรัฐบาล และสำหรับพวกเขาและพรรคกรีนที่จะสนับสนุนแพ็คเกจทั้งหมดที่เสนอ” Thand Ringqvist เขียน

title: How integration policies are becoming more stringent across Europe
desc:
Citizenship policy is increasingly used by governments in rich countries to define migrants’ “integration expectations,” according to a landmark report on international migration.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), an international organisation based in Paris that promotes the market economy and global trade, published this week its 50th annual international migration outlook.

The report shows a growing migration trend, and integration policy entering “a more constrained and politically contested phase”.

“Tight public budgets, pressure on housing and public services and weaker political appetite for broad-based integration investments have slowed reform and changed its character,” it continues.

Citizenship reforms that took place in 2025-2026 in many of the OECD’s 38 member countries are part of this picture. According to the study, they “point to more stringent conditions” with strengthened requirements on “language proficiency, civic knowledge, fiscal contribution, residence duration and self-sufficiency,” the report adds.
summary: Citizenship policy is increasingly used by governments in rich countries to define migrants’ “integration expectations,” according to a landmark report on international migration.
titleTh: นโยบายบูรณาการมีความเข้มงวดมากขึ้นทั่วยุโรปอย่างไร
descTh:
รัฐบาลในประเทศร่ำรวยมีการใช้นโยบายความเป็นพลเมืองมากขึ้นเพื่อกำหนด "ความคาดหวังในการบูรณาการ" ของผู้ย้ายถิ่น ตามรายงานสำคัญเกี่ยวกับการย้ายถิ่นระหว่างประเทศ

องค์การเพื่อความร่วมมือทางเศรษฐกิจและการพัฒนา (OECD) ซึ่งเป็นองค์กรระหว่างประเทศที่ตั้งอยู่ในกรุงปารีส ซึ่งส่งเสริมเศรษฐกิจตลาดและการค้าโลก เผยแพร่แนวโน้มการย้ายถิ่นฐานระหว่างประเทศประจำปีครั้งที่ 50 ในสัปดาห์นี้

รายงานดังกล่าวแสดงให้เห็นถึงแนวโน้มการย้ายถิ่นที่เพิ่มขึ้น และนโยบายบูรณาการกำลังเข้าสู่ "ช่วงที่มีข้อจำกัดมากขึ้นและมีการโต้แย้งทางการเมืองมากขึ้น"

“งบประมาณสาธารณะที่จำกัด ความกดดันต่อที่อยู่อาศัยและบริการสาธารณะ และความกระหายทางการเมืองที่อ่อนแอลงสำหรับการลงทุนบูรณาการในวงกว้าง ได้ชะลอการปฏิรูปและเปลี่ยนลักษณะของมัน” รายงานกล่าวต่อ

การปฏิรูปความเป็นพลเมืองที่เกิดขึ้นในปี 2568-2569 ในหลายประเทศสมาชิกของ OECD 38 ประเทศเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของภาพนี้ จากการศึกษาพบว่า พวกเขา "ชี้ให้เห็นถึงเงื่อนไขที่เข้มงวดมากขึ้น" โดยมีข้อกำหนดที่เข้มงวดมากขึ้นเกี่ยวกับ "ความสามารถทางภาษา ความรู้ของพลเมือง เงินสมทบทางการคลัง ระยะเวลาที่อยู่อาศัย และการพึ่งพาตนเอง" รายงานกล่าวเสริม

การปฏิรูปความเป็นพลเมืองที่เกิดขึ้นในปี 2568-2569 ในหลายประเทศสมาชิกของ OECD 38 ประเทศเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของภาพนี้ จากการศึกษาพบว่า พวกเขา "ชี้ให้เห็นถึงเงื่อนไขที่เข้มงวดมากขึ้น" โดยมีข้อกำหนดที่เข้มงวดมากขึ้นเกี่ยวกับ "ความสามารถทางภาษา ความรู้ของพลเมือง เงินสมทบทางการคลัง ระยะเวลาที่อยู่อาศัย และการพึ่งพาตนเอง" รายงานกล่าวเสริม

title: How integration policies are becoming more stringent across Europe
desc:
Citizenship policy is increasingly used by governments in rich countries to define migrants’ “integration expectations,” according to a landmark report on international migration.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), an international organisation based in Paris that promotes the market economy and global trade, published this week its 50th annual international migration outlook.

The report shows a growing migration trend, and integration policy entering “a more constrained and politically contested phase”.

“Tight public budgets, pressure on housing and public services and weaker political appetite for broad-based integration investments have slowed reform and changed its character,” it continues.

Citizenship reforms that took place in 2025-2026 in many of the OECD’s 38 member countries are part of this picture. According to the study, they “point to more stringent conditions” with strengthened requirements on “language proficiency, civic knowledge, fiscal contribution, residence duration and self-sufficiency,” the report adds.
summary: Citizenship policy is increasingly used by governments in rich countries to define migrants’ “integration expectations,” according to a landmark report on international migration.
